articles.title: Seamless Carbon and Alloy Steel Standard, Line, and Pressure Pipe From Georgia and India; Institution of Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Investigations and Scheduling of Preliminary Phase Investigations
articles.summary: The Commission hereby gives notice of the institution of investigations and commencement of preliminary phase antidumping and countervailing duty investigation Nos. 701-TA-810 and 731-TA-1811-1812 (Preliminary) pursuant to the Tariff Act of 1930 to determine whether there is a reasonable indication that an industry in the United States is materially injured or threatened with material injury, or the establishment of an industry in the United States is materially retarded, by reason of imports of...
articles.full_text: The Commission hereby gives notice of the institution of investigations and commencement of preliminary phase antidumping and countervailing duty investigation Nos. 701-TA-810 and 731-TA-1811-1812 (Preliminary) pursuant to the Tariff Act of 1930 to determine whether there is a reasonable indication that an industry in the United States is materially injured or threatened with material injury, or the establishment of an industry in the United States is materially retarded, by reason of imports of seamless carbon and alloy steel standard, line, and pressure pipe from Georgia and India, provided for in subheadings 7304.19.10, 7304.19.50, 7304.31.60, 7304.39.00, 7304.51.50, 7304.59.60, and 7304.59.80 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States, that are alleged to be sold in the United States at less than fair value and alleged to be subsidized by the Government of India. Unless the Department of Commerce ("Commerce") extends the time for initiation, the Commission must reach a preliminary determination in antidumping and countervailing duty investigations in 45 days, or in this case by November 30, 2026. The Commission's views must be transmitted to Commerce within five business days thereafter, or by December 7, 2026.

AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
DATES:
Applicable October 20, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Natasia Byrd and Andrew Hart at (202) 482-1240 and (202) 482-1058, respectively (the People's Republic of China (China)), Ted Pearson and Ethan Lewis at (202) 482-2631 and (202) 482-4046, respectively (India), and Catherine Bonilla at (202) 482-7955 (Mexico), AD/CVD Operations, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On September 8, 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) initiated countervailing duty (CVD) investigations of imports of certain linear hydraulic cylinders and parts thereof (hydraulic cylinders) from China, India, and Mexico.[1]
Currently, the preliminary determinations are due no later than November 12, 2026.
Postponement of Preliminary Determinations
Section 703(b)(1) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), requires Commerce to issue the preliminary determination in a countervailing duty investigation within 65 days after the date on which Commerce initiated the investigation. However, section 703(c)(1) of the Act permits Commerce to postpone the preliminary determination in a CVD investigation until no later than 130 days after the date on which Commerce initiated the investigation if: (A) the petitioner makes a timely request for a postponement; or
( printed page 66295)
(B) Commerce concludes that the parties concerned are cooperating, that the investigation is extraordinarily complicated, and that additional time is necessary to make a preliminary determination. Under 19 CFR 351.205(e), the petitioner must submit a request for postponement 25 days or more before the scheduled date of the preliminary determination and must state the reasons for the request. Commerce will grant the request unless it finds compelling reasons to deny the request.
On October 14, 2026, the petitioner [2]
timely requested that Commerce postpone the preliminary CVD determinations to 130 days from the date of initiation, pursuant to 19 CFR 351.205(b) and (e).[3]
The petitioner stated a postponement is warranted to provide Commerce with additional time to review and analyze questionnaire responses, and issue supplemental questionnaires prior to making preliminary CVD determinations.[4]
In accordance with 19 CFR 351.205(e), the petitioner has stated the reasons for requesting a postponement of the preliminary determinations, and Commerce finds no compelling reason to deny the request. Therefore, in accordance with section 703(c)(1)(A) of the Act, Commerce is postponing the deadline for the preliminary determinations in the CVD investigations of hydraulic cylinders from China, India, and Mexico to no later than 130 days after the date on which these investigations were initiated,
i.e.,
January 19, 2027.[5]
Pursuant to section 705(a)(1) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.210(b)(1), the deadline for the final determinations of these investigations will continue to be 75 days after the date of the preliminary determinations.
Notification to Interested Parties
This notice is issued and published pursuant to section 703(c)(2) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.205(f)(1).
Dated: October 16, 2026.
Scot Fullerton,
Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary for Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Operations.

The petitioner is the Hydraulic Cylinders Fair Trade Coalition, whose members are Aggressive Hydraulics Inc., Hol-Mac Corporation, Ligon Hydraulics, Prince Manufacturing Corporation, PTC, Alliance LLC, Rosenboom Machine & Tool Inc., Scot Industries Inc., Stillwell Inc., and Texas Hydraulics Inc.

articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
                    ACTION:
Notice; correction.
                    SUMMARY:
                        The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) published notice in the 
                        Federal Register
                         of May 22, 2025, in which Commerce issued the antidumping duty (AD) orders on dioctyl terephthalate (DOTP) from Malaysia, Poland, Taiwan, and the Republic of Türkiye (Türkiye). The notice incorrectly stated the dates of the ending of provisional measures and the termination of suspension of liquidation due to the expiration of provisional measures.
                    
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
                    On May 22, 2025, Commerce published in the 
                    Federal Register
                     the AD orders on DOTP from Malaysia, Poland, Taiwan, and Türkiye.[] 
                    
                     In the “Provisional Measures” section of that notice, we: (1) incorrectly stated that the six-month provisional measures period beginning on the date of the publication of the 
                    Preliminary Determinations
                     ended on May 4, 2025; and (2) incorrectly stated that the termination of suspension of liquidation due to the expiration of provisional measures began on May 5, 2025. The correct dates for the end of provisional measures and the termination of suspension of liquidation as a result of the expiration of provisional measures are May 3, 2025, and May 4, 2025, respectively.
                
Correction
                    In the 
                    Federal Register
                     of May 22, 2025, in FR Doc 2025-09163, on page 21899, in the first column, correct the following sentences to read as follows: “Therefore, the six-month provisional measures period beginning on the date of publication of the 
                    Preliminary Determinations
                     ended on May 3, 2025” and “. . . DOTP from Malaysia, Poland, Taiwan, and Türkiye entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after May 4, 2025.”
                
Notification to Interested Parties
This notice is issued and published in accordance with section 736(a) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, and 19 CFR 351.211(b).
                    Dated: October 15, 2026.
Scot Fullerton,
Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary for Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Operations.

articles.title: Ecoprogetti CEO: Global Solar Supply Chains Shift Toward Protectionism as India Leads Industrial Policy - IndexBox
articles.summary: Ecoprogetti CEO: Global Solar Supply Chains Shift Toward Protectionism as India Leads Industrial Policy  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
India Becomes World's Second-Largest Solar Market
India overtook the US to become the world's second-largest solar market in 2025, adding nearly 50 GW, with analysts forecasting continued expansion of 526 GW.
Global solar supply chains are shifting toward protectionism and industrial policies designed to support domestic manufacturing, according to an interview with pv magazine featuring Laura Sartore, CEO of Italian solar machinery and production line specialist Ecoprogetti. Sartore told the publication that every major supply chain worldwide except China is moving toward some form of protectionism and price floors, with the United States among the most prominent examples.
According to Sartore, the US market demonstrates that minimum price thresholds, even when set above the prices charged by Chinese manufacturers, do not necessarily slow demand. She indicated that the sector continues to grow despite higher component costs, supported by the development of a domestic supply chain. In China, prices are also rising gradually across the supply chain after government efforts to curb overcapacity, a trend that was expected to continue into 2025. Sartore said this reflects a growing focus on the economic viability of manufacturing in a market where solar technology has already established its competitiveness against other energy sources.
Sartore identified India as one of the most compelling examples of industrial policy in the solar sector. The Indian government is progressively expanding protectionist measures and domestic manufacturing requirements beyond modules to include cells, wafers and ingots, aiming to reduce dependence on Chinese imports and strengthen local production capacity. Sartore said India has the most serious industrial policy, having observed Europe's mistakes and continuing to monitor developments in the United States, and she highlighted the clear industrial strategy of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.
A key element of that strategy is industry consolidation. Production capacity exceeding domestic demand is not necessarily seen as a problem and can instead encourage mergers and direct investment toward underdeveloped segments of the supply chain. Sartore said the era of small factories with 200-500 MW of capacity is over and that multi-gigawatt-scale facilities are now emerging, which she described as the only way forward for a continent-sized nation like India. This consolidation is helping create larger, more financially robust manufacturers able to invest not only in cell and module production but also in materials and components such as glass, encapsulants, backsheets and junction boxes.
According to Sartore, India now has the most comprehensive solar manufacturing supply chain outside China, though domestic polysilicon production remains underdeveloped. She explained that beyond raw material extraction, polysilicon production requires specialized technological expertise, capital-intensive facilities and competitive access to energy, capabilities she said are currently lacking and must be developed. She also stressed that India must aim for high environmental standards and low-emission processes from the outset rather than simply replicating capacity without prioritizing emissions, noting that these requirements could lengthen the timeline for building a domestic supply chain.
While India and the United States focus on large-scale factories and highly integrated supply chains, Sartore advocates a different approach for Europe. She argues that Europe's industrial model cannot be assessed by the same criteria applied in the United States or Asia, since the continent's manufacturing sector has historically been built around small and medium-sized enterprises, industrial clusters and networks of specialized manufacturers. She pointed to Italy and Germany, where industries have achieved international leadership through networks of relatively small but highly competitive companies, and said Europe's multi-factory, network-based model should not be abandoned.
This does not mean small module assembly lines can remain competitive regardless of capacity. Sartore said manufacturers need a minimum production scale and adequate investment in technology and automation to justify capital expenditure and maintain competitive costs, citing 800 MW to 1 GW as the minimum threshold for a sustainable investment. She identified 1 GW to 3 GW as offering an optimal balance between economies of scale, financial viability and operational complexity, typically corresponding to companies with annual revenue of EUR100 million to EUR200 million and roughly 150 to 300 employees.
Sartore noted that operating costs, particularly raw material procurement, present a challenge beyond initial capital investment. While increasing capacity initially reduces unit production costs, there is a point beyond which the financial burden of running a larger facility offsets those savings. She said that in the European context the 1 GW to 3 GW range captures economies of scale, while beyond 3 GW additional management costs and financial charges weigh on the bottom line without necessarily lowering raw material procurement costs. For a 5 GW factory, working capital requirements can become significant, requiring substantial credit lines, bank guarantees and careful financial planning, and larger facilities also face greater financial exposure if demand falls short of capacity.
Sartore explained that in Europe, without supply chain integration, purchasing 5 GW worth of raw materials would require structured bank collateral, with high costs for credit guarantees and interest on cash flow weighing on the purchase price and potentially making the resulting module no more cost-effective than one from a smaller manufacturer. She said a larger factory therefore does not necessarily have lower production costs than a medium-sized facility once financing expenses and operating overheads are considered, and that a more moderate scale can help medium-sized European manufacturers limit financial exposure and manage working capital.
Production capacity should also reflect market demand, according to Sartore. Europe's solar market is more fragmented than other major international markets, with projects generally smaller than gigawatt-scale installations and manufacturers required to handle a wider range of order sizes. European projects often range from a few megawatts to several tens of megawatts, while installations approaching or exceeding 1 GW remain relatively rare. Sartore said this supports a network of manufacturers able to adapt production to individual customer requirements, adding that Europe is unlikely to see many gigawatt-scale solar plant projects and that diverse requirements and local conditions make numerous medium-to-large plants more likely than many mega-installations. Production flexibility therefore becomes a key competitive factor alongside manufacturing costs and supply chain capabilities.
The dynamics shaping global photovoltaic supply chains, including modules, inverters and battery energy storage systems, are scheduled to be discussed during a session titled Decoding solar supply chains at the NetZero event in Milan on Oct. 21.

articles.summary: Why more Chinese firms are eyeing Thailand over Vietnam after trade war 2.0  South China Morning Post
articles.full_text:
In Focus‘Poster child’: why more Chinese firms have Thailand in their expansion plans
The Land of Smiles has become a prime location for Chinese businesses diversifying operations offshore, as Vietnam reaches saturation point
Vietnam, popular for much of this period, is beginning to lose some favour as firms look to Thailand as another alternative destination. The latter country has gained the edge on its competitor in the post-trade war 2.0 era, attracting billions of US dollars in outlays last year.
But the influx has also made Bangkok more mindful of risks, particularly those related to US measures intended to limit Chinese transshipment.

articles.title: Trump’s 50% Canada tariffs challenged in court - Supply Chain Dive
articles.summary: Trump’s 50% Canada tariffs challenged in court  Supply Chain Dive
articles.full_text:
A lawsuit filed this week is seeking the removal of tariffs on imports into the U.S. from Canada.
The suit, filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade Tuesday on behalf of food importing company Gellert Global Group, alleges that President Donald Trump overstepped his executive powers by implementing a 50% tariff on $20 billion worth of Canada goods earlier this year and that the trade policy disrupted supplier relationships while adding costs for the family-run business. The suit asks for the court to strike down the levies, block their collection and order refunds.
Trump relied on Section 338 of the Trade Act of 1930 to put the levies in place, a statute the lawsuit says has not been previously used to impose tariffs in the 96 years since it was enacted. Section 338 gives a president the power to levy tariffs of up to 50% in response to discrimination by another country on U.S. commerce. The suit argues Trump did not adequately identify Canadian policies that would justify the statute’s use while asserting that Section 338 is superseded by more recent regulations, namely Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. Trump has leveraged Section 301 to levy tariffs, which have also come under legal scrutiny.
The suit further contends that beyond failing to meet Section 338’s requirements, Trump improperly used the statute by placing tariffs on products not tied to alleged discrimination by Canada and later expanding the list of impacted products without adhering to a mandatory 30-day waiting period.
“No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required,” Sara Albrecht, chairman and CEO of the Liberty Justice Center, which filed the suit on behalf of Gellert, said in an Oct. 20 press release. The legal services firm has previously filed similar suits against other Trump administration tariffs.
The U.S. and Canada have been embroiled in a trade war since negotiations between the two countries broke down the day before 50% tariffs went into place on Aug. 22. Trump initially announced the levies in late July, sparking talks between the two trading partners. However, Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney ultimately called back his negotiators, noting that newly proposed terms wouldn’t have benefitted Canada. The country later implemented retaliatory tariffs in September. In response, Trump tagged more goods with the 50% tariff while instituting import bans on products such as motorcycles and beer.
“The fight is likely to center over the limits Congress put on that authority,” James Kim, an international trade partner at ArentFox Schiff, said in a LinkedIn post. “Were the Canadian measures discrimination under Section 338, or retaliation for U.S. tariffs? Those labels aren’t necessarily mutually exclusive; retaliation could still qualify as discrimination. And even if the statutory trigger was met, do those 50 percent actually offset the burden on U.S. commerce, as the statute requires?”
The lawsuit alleges the trade dispute has had a deleterious effect on Gellert, which relies on cross-border trade throughout the production process for certain cheeses. Trump added specialty cheeses to the list of goods impacted by the Section 338 tariffs in September.
“Gellert Global Group has spent generations building trusted relationships with suppliers, customers and partners across the food industry,” Thomas Gellert, co-CEO of Gellert Global Group, said in the release. “These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain.”
The Trump administration has faced several lawsuits from businesses and states over previous levies, such as those installed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA levies in February.
Similarly, the Court of International Trade in May ruled a temporary 10% tariff Trump instituted after the IEEPA decision was illegal. However, the Trump administration is appealing the ruling on the levies, which have since expired.
“I would say that this is likely a harder case for the challengers than IEEPA,” Kim said. “The Supreme Court held that IEEPA did not authorize tariffs. Section 338 expressly does. That makes a challenge to the basic tariff authority a steeper climb.”

articles.title: Vietnam just got zero tariffs in Europe. Latin American exporters should be worried. - Latin Times
articles.summary: Vietnam just got zero tariffs in Europe. Latin American exporters should be worried.  Latin Times
articles.full_text:
Vietnam did not wait for Latin America to catch up.
While South American and Mexican exporters were still absorbing the ripple effects of their own hard-won market openings, Hanoi moved — completing a sweeping trade pact with Europe's second commercial bloc one day after the rest of the world's attention was focused elsewhere. The consequences for Latin American manufacturers are not theoretical; they are structural, and they are already in motion.
A 14-Year Deal With Immediate Market Consequences
Vietnam and the European Free Trade Association formally concluded a comprehensive free trade agreement on October 18, 2026, in Hanoi, after fourteen years and 21 rounds of negotiations that began in 2012 and were interrupted for years before resuming in 2025. The ceremony brought together Lê Mạnh Hùng, Vietnam's Minister of Industry and Trade, who signed the document on Hanoi's behalf, alongside the heads of government of Norway, Switzerland, Iceland, and Liechtenstein.
President and General Secretary Tô Lâm — Vietnam's top leader, holding the country's two most powerful positions simultaneously — attended the Hanoi ceremony in person, a signal that this was not a routine trade formality but a presidential-level strategic commitment.
The scope of the agreement is broad: it addresses trade in goods and services, rules of origin, intellectual property rights, government procurement, investment, sanitary measures, and sustainable development. But it is the tariff architecture that carries the most immediate competitive weight.
Under the deal, EFTA members immediately liberalize more than 90% of tariff lines, representing 99.5% of Vietnam's current exports to the bloc. Covered products include textiles and garments, footwear, seafood, computers and electronic components, and machinery and equipment. Vietnamese agricultural goods — including rice, honey, and fruit — also receive tariff reductions. Selected European products such as cheese and chocolate will gain duty-free access to the Vietnamese market, but only after a transition period of up to 16 years.
The EFTA Prize: A $630 Billion Market With Room to Grow
The commercial opportunity at stake is considerable. EFTA's annual import turnover runs to roughly $630 billion, and Vietnamese goods currently account for just 0.65% of that figure. Bilateral trade between EFTA and Vietnam totaled €4.8 billion in 2025, with Vietnam running a €2.5 billion surplus — a gap that has widened sharply compared with a decade earlier.
For Colombian garment producers, Brazilian footwear exporters, and Mexican electronics assemblers competing for shelf space in Zurich or Oslo, the arithmetic is straightforward: their Vietnamese rivals now pay zero import duties, while Latin American goods still face standard EFTA tariff rates. The competitive floor has shifted, and there is no reversal mechanism built into the agreement.
The Mercosur Flank: Vietnam Takes the Competition South
The EFTA pact drew the headlines, but a simultaneous diplomatic push may ultimately prove more consequential for the region. Vietnam is negotiating directly with South America's largest economic bloc — not just for market access in Europe, but for preferential access to Mercosur's domestic markets themselves.
The first round of negotiations for the Vietnam–Mercosur Preferential Trade Agreement concluded on August 28, 2026, after five days of technical sessions in Buenos Aires, with Argentina coordinating the bloc's side. The framing on both ends was optimistic: Argentine officials highlighted that bilateral trade had doubled over the past decade, growing from approximately $6.6 billion in 2015 to more than $12 billion in 2025, without any preferential framework in place.
If a preferential deal is reached, the implications for Brazilian and Argentine manufacturers extend beyond export competition in third markets. Vietnamese electronics — which generated nearly $165 billion in export revenue in 2025 — would gain improved access to the Brazilian and Argentine consumer market, the very domestic revenue base that regional producers depend on when global export conditions tighten.
Latin American Textiles and Electronics Face a Structural Squeeze
For the textile sector on both continents, the combined effect of Vietnam's European trade moves represents a pincer movement.
Brazil's textile and apparel industry counts 25,700 businesses employing approximately 1.3 million workers and generating $40.9 billion in annual revenue. The sector had cautiously welcomed the EU–Mercosur agreement — signed in Asunción on January 17, 2026 — as a pathway to expanded European market access. Industry associations representing Brazilian manufacturers (ABIT), their Argentine counterparts (FITA), and Europe's own textile lobby (EURATEX) issued a joint statement in February calling the deal "essential" for competitiveness on both sides of the Atlantic.
Vietnam's EFTA deal partially neutralizes that advantage. European buyers who might have shifted sourcing toward Mercosur suppliers under the new EU framework now have an equally competitive Vietnamese alternative — one that operates under zero tariffs across both EU and EFTA channels simultaneously.
The overlap in export categories is not coincidental. Vietnam's textile and garment industry posted $46 billion in exports in 2025 and has set a $50 billion target for 2026, driven by the same European and American buyers that Latin American producers compete for. Vietnam is already the world's second-largest garment exporter. The EFTA deal adds one more preferential lane to a network that already covers most of its major trading partners.
Hanoi's Export Pivot and the U.S. Tariff Pressure
The aggressive pace of trade diversification is not a coincidence of timing. Vietnam has been under sustained pressure to reduce its dependence on the U.S. market, which absorbs roughly 30% of Vietnam's total exports. That reliance became a structural liability after Washington imposed reciprocal tariffs that left Vietnamese textile and garment exports facing a 12.5% U.S. import duty — 2.5 percentage points above the 10% rate applied to some regional competitors — according to the Vietnam Textile and Apparel Association.
Vietnam's response has been systematic: conclude the EFTA deal, push for EU-market access under the existing EU–Vietnam FTA (in force since 2020), and now open negotiations with Mercosur. Taken together, the strategy is to spread export volume across so many preferential lanes that no single market disruption — however large — can destabilize the country's export-driven growth model.
What Latin American Trade Ministries Must Reckon With Now
The Vietnam–Mercosur PTA remains at an early stage, and the EFTA deal must pass parliamentary ratification in each member country before entering full force. But direction matters as much as timeline in trade policy, and the direction here is unambiguous.
Vietnam is no longer simply an Asian competitor in Asian-facing supply chains. It is now an active rival in European markets — and a prospective entrant to South American domestic ones. For trade ministries from Bogotá to São Paulo, the question is no longer whether to respond; it is how fast a coordinated response can be assembled, and whether the advantages secured under the EU–Mercosur agreement will be enough to offset what Hanoi has just put in place.

articles.title: China proposes AI export controls, affecting open-weight models - ET Datacenters
articles.summary: China proposes AI export controls, affecting open-weight models  ET Datacenters
articles.full_text:
AI agents, chip designs, and computing clusters. This proposal raises questions about the future availability of Chinese open-weight models outside the country, according to the Associated Press.
For Indian businesses using models from Chinese companies such as DeepSeek and Alibaba, the controls could introduce uncertainty over future releases. They may also affect overseas deployment and commercial use.
The proposed restrictions cover core AI models trained using important Chinese data. These models must meet computing requirements of 10-to-the-power-26 floating-point operations (FLOPs) or have two trillion parameters or more. They also include models ranking among the world's top 10 on relevant leaderboards, as reported by the South China Morning Post (SCMP).
The draft also covers AI agents designed for sensitive environments, including national defence and critical information infrastructure. Chip designs and computing clusters are also included.
The public consultation on the draft runs until November 15, 2026. The final rules will determine which technologies require approval and how licensing requirements apply to overseas transfers.
Impact on Open-Weight AI Ecosystem
Open-weight AI models make their trained parameters, or weights, available for others to download and run. Developers can use these models on their own infrastructure, fine-tune them, and integrate them into applications.
Chinese developers have become important suppliers of open-weight models. DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen, and models from Moonshot AI and Z.ai are among the options for developers. The proposed controls could complicate overseas access to some of these models if transferring their weights from China requires regulatory approval.
Alex Colville, an analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, told the SCMP that new compliance requirements could delay or prevent Chinese AI companies from partnering with global cloud providers. This could affect the deployment of their most capable open-weight models overseas.
A spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce told the SCMP that licensing for open-source AI technologies would be expedited with immediate clearance upon filing. However, Colville noted that the practical meaning of this process remained unclear.
This distinction matters for enterprises that have already integrated models such as DeepSeek or Qwen into their applications. The proposal does not, by itself, establish that these deployments must be discontinued.

articles.title: EFTA and Vietnam sign trade agreement with major tariff cuts for Norway - London Daily News
articles.summary: EFTA and Vietnam sign trade agreement with major tariff cuts for Norway  London Daily News
articles.full_text:
Norway and the three other members of the European Free Trade Association have signed a broad free-trade agreement with Vietnam, setting out a staged reduction in duties on Norwegian exports and new commitments covering services, investment and sustainable development. The agreement was signed in Hanoi on 18 October by representatives of Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein and Vietnam’s Minister of Industry and Trade.
Seafood tariffs to fall in stages
The agreement’s clearest near-term commercial change for Norway concerns seafood. Vietnam currently applies tariffs of up to 15 per cent to Norwegian salmon and mackerel. Under the agreed schedule, salmon is to enter Vietnam duty-free when the agreement takes effect. Mackerel is to reach zero duty after a three-year phase-down.
The changes are not yet in force. The signing establishes the agreed terms, but the official announcements describe the tariff benefits as conditional on the agreement entering into force. Businesses should therefore distinguish the negotiated timetable from current customs treatment. The precise effect on an exporter will also depend on the product, origin requirements and the timing of implementation.
Norway’s government says roughly half of its exports to Vietnam will become duty-free when the agreement enters into force. More than 98 per cent are expected to be duty-free within seven years. The figure refers to exports covered by the agreement’s tariff schedule; it does not mean that all goods become duty-free immediately, nor does it guarantee that Norwegian firms will increase sales.
A wider framework for trade
The agreement reaches beyond customs duties on goods. Its chapters address trade in services and investment, alongside rules of origin, sanitary and technical requirements, intellectual property, trade remedies and government procurement. It also includes provisions for small and medium-sized businesses, cooperation and capacity-building, and trade and sustainable development.
Rules of origin determine whether a product qualifies for preferential treatment by establishing where it was made or sufficiently transformed. They matter because a lower tariff is available only to goods that meet the relevant conditions. For companies operating supply chains across several countries, documentation and sourcing decisions can be as important as the headline tariff rate.
The services and investment provisions are intended to provide a framework for commercial activity beyond shipments of physical products. They may be relevant to firms seeking to sell expertise or establish operations across borders, although the agreement’s signature alone does not establish how many businesses will use those opportunities. The sustainable-development chapter makes those issues part of the trade framework rather than limiting the deal to market access.
Trade ties and the next steps
Norwegian goods trade with Vietnam was worth about 19 billion Norwegian kroner in 2025, according to the Norwegian government. Across all four EFTA states, trade with Vietnam totalled 4.8 billion euros that year, according to EFTA. These figures describe different groupings and currencies and should not be directly compared as if they measured the same trade flows.
Electrical machinery, fish, pharmaceuticals and mechanical machinery were among EFTA’s leading exports to Vietnam in 2025. Vietnam’s leading exports to EFTA included electrical machinery, footwear, apparel and mechanical machinery. The scale and mix of existing trade help explain why the agreement covers both tariff treatment and the rules that shape cross-border business.
The deal follows a long negotiation process, launched in 2012 and concluded in July 2026. Its signing is a significant step in the relationship between Vietnam and the four EFTA states, but the practical changes will come only when the agreement enters into force. Until then, exporters and importers must continue to operate under the existing arrangements.
For Norwegian seafood producers, the agreed schedule offers a defined route to duty-free access for salmon and, later, mackerel. For other businesses, the agreement sets out a broader framework intended to make trade and investment more predictable. Whether that framework leads to stronger commercial links will depend on implementation and on companies’ ability to meet the agreement’s terms.

AGENCY:
Department of the Navy, Department of Defense.
ACTION:
Notice of Issuance of Certificate of Alternate Compliance.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Navy hereby announces that a Certificate of Alternate Compliance has been issued for USS PATRICK GALLAGHER (DDG 127). Due to the special construction and purpose of this vessel, the Admiralty Counsel of the Navy has determined it is a vessel of the Navy which, due to its special construction and purpose, cannot comply fully with the navigation lights provisions of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972 (72 COLREGS) without interfering with its special function as a naval ship. The intended effect of this notice is to warn mariners in waters where 72 COLREGS apply.
DATES:
This Certificate of Alternate Compliance is effective October 20, 2026 and is applicable beginning April 23, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Lieutenant Commander Jordan Foley, JAGC, U.S. Navy, Admiralty Attorney, Office of the Judge Advocate General, Admiralty and Claims Division (Code 15A), 1322 Patterson Ave. SE, Suite 3000, Washington Navy Yard, DC 20374-5066, 202-685-5040, or
admiralty@us.navy.mil.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background and Purpose. Executive Order (E.O.) 11964 (42 FR 4327; January 19, 1977) and 33 U.S.C. 1605 provide that the requirements of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972 (72 COLREGS), as to the number, position, range, or arc of visibility of lights or shapes, as well as to the disposition and characteristics of sound-signaling appliances, shall not
( printed page 66320)
apply to a vessel or class of vessels of the Navy where the Secretary of the Navy shall find and certify that, by reason of special construction or purpose, it is not possible for such vessel(s) to comply fully with the provisions without interfering with the special function of the vessel(s). Notice of issuance of a Certificate of Alternate Compliance must be made in the
Federal Register
.
In accordance with 33 U.S.C. 1605, the Admiralty Counsel of the Navy, under authority delegated by the Secretary of the Navy, hereby finds and certifies that USS PATRICK GALLAGHER (DDG 127) is a vessel of special construction or purpose, and that, with respect to the position of the following navigational lights, it is not possible to comply fully with the requirements of the provisions enumerated in the 72 COLREGS without interfering with the special function of the vessel: Annex I, paragraph 3(a), pertaining to the position of the forward masthead light; Annex I, paragraph 2(f)(i) pertaining to the vertical position of the aft masthead light; Annex I, paragraph 3(a), pertaining to the horizontal distance between the masthead lights; Annex I, paragraph 3(c), pertaining to the horizontal distance of the “task lights” below the masthead lights; Annex I, paragraph 2(f)(ii), pertaining to the horizontal position of the task lights above the aft masthead light(s) and vertical position of the task lights between the forward masthead light(s) and aft masthead light(s).
The Admiralty Counsel of the Navy further finds and certifies that these navigational lights are in closest possible compliance with the applicable provision of the 72 COLREGS.

articles.title: Beijing blasts US sanctions on 5 Chinese firms tied to ex-Google engineer - AP News
articles.summary: Beijing blasts US sanctions on 5 Chinese firms tied to ex-Google engineer  AP NewsUS Sanctions China’s Y Combinator in Google AI Secrets Case  Bloomberg.comImposing Sanctions to Protect Americans from Intellectual Property Theft Fact Sheet  U.S. Department of State (.gov)United States China Sanctions  GazetteXtraU.S. Sanctions Five Chinese Entities Linked to Google AI Trade Secret Theft  The Information
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Beijing on Tuesday expressed “firm opposition” to the Trump administration’s sanctions on five Chinese companies connected to a former Google engineer accused of intellectual property theft.
The move “severely harms the legitimate rights and interests” of Chinese businesses, the country’s commerce ministry said in a statement. “The nature of this act is egregious. China firms opposes this.”
The ministry also urged the U.S. to “correct its erroneous practice” and said Beijing would take “necessary measures,” without specifying them.
It came a day after the U.S. State Department imposed sanctions on five Chinese companies connected to Linwei Ding, who founded Shanghai Zhisuan Technology. The department said he had touted his experience with Google and claimed his company could replicate the American tech giant’s super intelligence infrastructure technology.
The startup incubation program MiraclePlus, which was sanctioned along with Zhisuan, gave seed capital in exchange for an ownership stake in Zhisuan, the State Department said. The other three Chinese entities facing penalties are linked to MiraclePlus.
Zhisuan “has knowingly engaged in, or benefitted from, significant theft of trade secrets of United States persons, which occurred on or after January 5, 2023,” the State Department said.
Ding was charged in 2024 with stealing artificial intelligence trade secrets from Google while secretly working with two companies based in China. In January, he was convicted by a federal jury in San Francisco of several counts of economic espionage and theft of trade secrets.
A judge later dismissed the economic espionage charges and sentenced him to 12 months in prison. The Justice Department is appealing the dismissal of the economic espionage charges.
China’s commerce ministry said its AI development is “the result of long-term cultivation in basic research, continuous innovation investment, and adherence to independent scientific and technological innovation and open cooperation.”
The country’s achievements have “nothing to do with the so-called ‘stealing of trade secrets,’” the ministry said.
___
Associated Press writer Eric Tucker contributed to this report.

Texas LNG asks DOE to amend its existing authorization to export domestically produced liquefied natural gas (LNG) to non-free trade agreement countries set forth in DOE/FE Order No. 4489 (as amended)—specifically, to extend its current export commencement deadline. On February 10, 2020, in DOE/FE Order No. 4489, as amended,[1]
DOE's Office of Fossil Energy (now known as the Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy Office) [2]
authorized Texas LNG to export domestically produced LNG by vessel from the proposed Texas LNG Brownsville LLC Liquefied Natural Gas Export Project (Project), to be located at the Port of Brownsville, Texas, to any country with which the United States has not entered into a free trade agreement (FTA) requiring national treatment for trade in natural gas, and with which trade is not prohibited by U.S. law or policy (non-FTA countries), pursuant to Natural Gas Act section 3(a).[3]
Texas LNG is authorized to export this LNG in a volume equivalent to 204.4 billion cubic feet (Bcf) per year (Bcf/yr) of natural gas for a term extending through December 31, 2050.[4]
Under Order No. 4489, Texas LNG is required to “commence export operations using the planned Project no later than seven years from the date of issuance of this Order”—
i.e.,
by February 10, 2027.[5]
In the Request, Texas LNG asks DOE to extend this export commencement deadline by five years, to February 10, 2032.[6]
In support of this Request, Texas LNG states that, in the period since the issuance of Order No. 4489, Texas LNG has proceeded actively and diligently to develop the Project toward a positive final investment decision (FID).[7]
Texas LNG states, however, that those good faith efforts have been “substantially frustrated” by extenuating circumstances outside of Texas LNG's control, most significantly due to six years of sustained litigation and remand proceedings challenging Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's (FERC's) authorization to site, construct and operate the Project by a joint group of opponents.[8]
Texas LNG states that “[t]his uncertainty made it more difficult for Texas LNG to secure the long-term financing and commercial commitments necessary to reach FID and meet its current export commencement deadline.” [9]
Texas LNG adds that, on August 21, 2025, the FERC granted Texas LNG's request for an extension of its existing construction and in-service deadline for the Project until November 22, 2029.[10]
Texas LNG asserts that the requested commencement extension until February 10, 2032, will provide Texas LNG with additional time after FERC's current construction and in-service deadline to execute commercial commitments and begin exports.[11]
Additionally, Texas LNG asks DOE to authorize an additional three-year make-up period at the end of its existing
( printed page 66323)
export authorization term through December 31, 2050, consistent with recent DOE practice.[12]
In reviewing the Request, DOE will consider any issues required by law or policy under NGA section 3(a), DOE's regulations, and any other documents deemed appropriate.
Parties that may oppose the Request should address these issues and documents in their comments and/or protests, as well as other issues deemed relevant to the Request.

requires DOE to give appropriate consideration to the environmental effects of its proposed decisions. No final decision will be issued in this proceeding until DOE has met its NEPA responsibilities.

AGENCY:
Office of Electricity, Department of Energy.
ACTION:
Notice of application.
SUMMARY:
Clear Power LLC (the Applicant or Clear Power) has applied for authorization to transmit electric energy from the United States to Mexico pursuant to the Federal Power Act.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before November 19, 2026.
The United States Department of Energy (DOE) regulates electricity exports from the United States to foreign countries in accordance with section 202(e) of the Federal Power Act (FPA) (16 U.S.C. 824a(e)) and regulations thereunder (10 CFR 205.300). Sections 301(b) and 402(f) of the DOE Organization Act (42 U.S.C. 7151(b) and 7172(f)) transferred this regulatory authority, previously exercised by the now-defunct Federal Power Commission, to DOE.
Section 202(e) of the FPA provides that an entity which seeks to export electricity must obtain an order from DOE authorizing that export (16 U.S.C. 824a(e)). On January 8, 2026, the authority to issue such orders was delegated to the DOE's Assistant Secretary for the Office of Electricity by Redelegation Order No. S3-DEL-OE1-2026.
On April 16, 2026, Clear Power filed an application (Application or App.) with DOE for renewal of export authority to transmit electric energy from the United States to Mexico for an additional five-year term. App. at 1. Clear Power was originally granted export authorization under Order No. EA-487 on December 9, 2020, which expired on December 9, 2025. Since Clear Power did not apply for renewal until after the expiration of the current export authorization, DOE is processing the application as a request for a new export authorization.
According to the Application, Clear Power is a limited liability corporation with its principal place of business in Folsom, California. The Applicant is a power marketer with “authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to market electric energy and capacity at wholesale pursuant to market-based rate authorization.”
Id.
at 2. Clear Power states that it is a “wholly-owned subsidiary of the Alaywan Trust, which owns or is affiliated with entities that own or control a combined total of 18.0 MW (nameplate) of operating renewable generation facilities all located in the California Independent System Operator (CAISO) market.”
Id.
Clear Power “does not own or control any electric power generation, transmission distribution facilities” and “does not have a franchised service area”
Id.
at 3. Thus, the Applicant states that it has “no `transmission system' of its own on which power exports could have a reliability or stability impact.”
Id.
at 5. Clear Power “will schedule its exports from the U.S. in compliance with all applicable reliability criteria, standards and guides as are set out by the North American Electricity Reliability Corporation (NERC) (or any successor organization), the North American Energy Standards Board (or any successor organization) and regional reliability councils and as applied by U.S. transmission providers.”
Id.
at 5-6.
The existing international transmission facilities to be utilized by the Applicant have been previously authorized by Presidential permits issued pursuant to Executive Order 10485, as amended, and are appropriate for open access transmission by third parties.
See
App. at Exhibit C.
Procedural Matters:
Any person desiring to be heard in this proceeding should file a comment to the Application at
Electricity.Exports@hq.doe.gov.
Comments concerning Clear Power's Application should be clearly marked with OE Docket No. EA-531. Comments will be posted along with the relevant application on the program website at
www.energy.gov/oe/pending-applications.
A final decision will be made on the requested authorization after the environmental impacts have been evaluated consistent with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA), as amended (42 U.S.C. 4321,
et seq.), the DOE NEPA regulations at 10 CFR part 1021, and the DOE's NEPA
( printed page 66322)
Implementing Procedures (June 2026) and after DOE evaluates whether the proposed action will have an adverse impact on the sufficiency of supply or reliability of the United States electric power supply system.

articles.title: New lawsuit filed challenging Trump’s tariffs on Canada - larongeNOW
articles.summary: New lawsuit filed challenging Trump’s tariffs on Canada  larongeNOW
articles.full_text:
A U.S. food importer has filed a lawsuit in the United States Court of International Trade challenging U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs targeting Canada.
The lawsuit, filed Tuesday by the non-profit Liberty Justice Center on behalf of Gellert Global Group in the New York-based court, argued Trump’s use of a Depression-era trade statute exceeds his power as president.
“No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required,” Liberty Justice Center CEO Sara Albrecht said in a news release.
Trump used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap an array of Canadian goods with a 50 per cent levy after trade talks broke down in August.

articles.title: US State Department Identifies Forced Labor in Chilean Agriculture and Aquaculture - elciudadano.com
articles.summary: US State Department Identifies Forced Labor in Chilean Agriculture and Aquaculture  elciudadano.com
articles.full_text:
Original article: Departamento de Estado de EEUU reconoce trata de personas con fines de trabajo forzoso en la agricultura y acuicultura chilenas
US State Department Identifies Forced Labor in Chilean Agriculture and Aquaculture
The United States Department of State has released its 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report, stating in its chapter on Chile that «traffickers exploit adults and children in forced labor in mining; agriculture, including the harvest of berries; aquaculture; construction; street vending; domestic work, and the hospitality, restaurant, and garment sectors.»
This acknowledgment is not isolated. Aquaculture has been highlighted in Chile’s profile in the report since at least 2023, and berry harvesting was added in 2025.
For Fundación Libera and the Ecoceanos Center, this reiteration confirms the documentation provided by workers, unions, and civil society organizations regarding forced labor in the salmon farming industry and export agriculture.
This evidence was presented by Fundación Libera and Ecoceanos to the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) during its Section 301 investigations concerning forced labor in Chile (files USTR-2026-0265 and USTR-2026-0266).
«The State Department officially recognizes what we have documented before the USTR: forced labor exists in Chilean agriculture and aquaculture. The Chilean State can no longer treat this as a mere accusation from civil society; it is an official diagnosis that requires concrete responses,» stated Carolina Rudnick Vizcarra, president of Fundación Libera.
Chile Maintains Level 1 Status
The report keeps Chile at Level 1 (countries whose governments fully meet the minimum standards of the U.S. Trafficking Victims Protection Act – TVPA – for the elimination of trafficking in persons), noting increased investigations, prosecutions, and identified victims. However, the same document reveals significant gaps regarding forced labor:
No Convictions for Forced Labor. In 2025, there were 816 investigations into trafficking: 644 for commercial sexual exploitation of minors (ESCNNA), 109 sexual trafficking cases, and only 62 for labor trafficking (7.6%). Fourteen people were prosecuted for forced labor, but all 34 convictions were for sexual exploitation.
Prosecutors Unaware of Forced Labor Problems: The report states that police officials, prosecutors, and the judicial sector lack a thorough understanding of human trafficking, and some local prosecutors fail to recognize the crime, particularly forced labor, nor do they gather sufficient evidence to support it. Deficiencies in evidence collection have also led authorities to pursue trafficking offenses under other articles of the Penal Code that impose lesser penalties than those provided in Article 411.
Unregulated Labor Recruiters: The report indicates that Chile does not regulate recruiters or hold them accountable for fraudulent recruitment, a critical link in the mediation and subcontracting processes in agriculture and salmon farming.
Specialized Capacity Lacking in the South: Specialized units of the PDI (Investigative Police) are located in Arica, Iquique, and Santiago; none in the regions where agriculture and salmon farming are concentrated. There are also no shelters for male victims.
Victims Without Support: Only 58 of the 245 identified victims (about 24%) received services, and there are limited spaces, challenges for specialized care, and territorial gaps in service availability, including a lack of shelters for male victims.
Punishments That Do Not Deter: The report outlines a consistent pattern of light and suspended sentences for crimes.
Policy Without Support: The National Action Plan Against Trafficking 2023–2026 has not been approved by the Presidency, and the Intersectoral Committee on Trafficking in Persons does not have its own budget.
«Processing only 14 people for forced labor, with none convicted, shows that the problem is not a lack of cases, but a system unprepared to recognize them. Until forced labor is an autonomous crime in Chile, it will continue to slip between criminal categories,» warned Carolina Rudnick.
Gaps in Labor Legislation and Government Inaction
Fundación Libera and the Ecoceanos Center have also raised concerns about the lack of labor legislation in high-risk sectors, which undermines the government’s claims about having strong legislation and institutions in place.
«In the same year that the State Department recognizes forced labor in Chile’s aquaculture, the government withdrew regulations that were supposed to enforce protections for subcontracted divers in salmon farming, according to Law 21.789,» questioned Juan Carlos Cárdenas, director of Ecoceanos.
«Without regulations, the law remains on paper, and contracting companies continue without enforceable obligations. Divers are exposed to excessive working hours, forced work during closed ports, and fear of retaliation if they refuse, indicators of forced labor according to the ILO,» he added.
Additionally, between 2013 and 2026, 91 worker deaths have been documented in this mega exporting industry: «Every month of delay deepens the lack of protection and the risk of exploitation; we demand the immediate return of the regulations to the General Comptroller’s Office,» stated the Ecoceanos director.
Requests from Fundación Libera and Centro Ecoceanos to the Chilean State
These are the proposals put forward by both organizations:
1) Criminalize forced labor according to international standards.
2) Strengthen sectoral labor legislation in high-risk forced labor sectors: Expedite the regulation of Law No. 21.789 (Diving Law), which protects subcontracted divers in salmon farming, and repeal the directive by the Labor Directorate that prevents undocumented migrants from filing complaints.
3) Implement a national prohibition on the importation of forced labor.
4) Eliminate restrictions on freedom of association and collective bargaining.
5) Enhance compliance with labor legislation.
6) Include transparent monitoring mechanisms and binding obligations in labor agreements within trade treaties.
7) Involve expert civil society organizations and victims in the design and implementation of public policy.
8) Create specialized investigative and prosecutorial capacity in the southern regions and designate prosecutors specifically for trafficking cases.
9) Ensure services and accommodations for all victims, including men and those outside the capital, and guarantee effective payment of reparations.
10) Approve and fund a new National Action Plan Against Trafficking, with its own budget for the Intersectoral Committee.
11) Approve and fund the National Action Plan Against Forced Labor, with its own budget for the Ministerial Advisory Commission for the Elimination of Forced Labor.
We will continue to provide updates. Cover Photo: Reference.

articles.title: Posthaste: Trump's tariffs can inflict far worse damage on the economy than just a recession, warns economist - Financial Post
articles.summary: Posthaste: Trump's tariffs can inflict far worse damage on the economy than just a recession, warns economist  Financial Post
articles.full_text:
Jimmy Jean, chief economist of the Desjardins Group, said many Canadian businesses adopted a wait-and-see approach to the turmoil of the first year of Trump’s term, but by early 2026 the mood shifted and companies began to find their footing again despite the uncertainty.
However, August brought another blow in the breakdown in trade talks, followed by a new tariff on about $27.6 billion in goods that did not include a carveout for products under the Canada-United-States-Mexico-Agreement. The Canadian counter tariffs that followed added more pressure.
Jean said though Trump’s new tariffs only affect 5 per cent of Canadian exports, their significance extends beyond the targeted goods.
“If businesses increasingly view the deterioration in Canada–U.S. trade relations as lasting rather than temporary, some may finally make decisions they had previously been willing to postpone,” he said in a report.
Some will adapt to the new environment by diversifying their export markets or supplies and investing to refocus their operations, he said. Others will cut production, cancel expansion projects or close facilities.
“In other words, moving from wait-and-see to adaptation doesn’t necessarily signal better days ahead. In some cases, adapting may mean permanently scaling back operations,” said Jean.
The economist said that’s why it’s important to focus on the structural effects of the trade war, rather than obsessing about a recession. Tariffs affect a limited share of the economy and other forces such as stronger energy revenues and public spending may continue to support growth.
“But avoiding a recession doesn’t mean the economy will emerge from the trade conflict unscathed,” he said.
In a typical recession weaker demand lowers economic activity and raises unemployment, but productive capacity remains largely intact and can be revived by support from the Bank of Canada and government.
But when factories close permanently and investments are abandoned, the damage to the economy extends beyond the 18 months of a recession and recovery, he said.
And that damage can be substantial. If the growth rate of an economy was reduced from two per cent to one, in five years its output would be nearly 5 per cent below what it otherwise would have been, he said.
In January the Bank of Canada estimated the country’s GDP would be 1.5 per cent lower at the end of this year than its forecast before the trade war. About half of that shortfall was attributed to lower output rather than just weaker demand, said Jean, showing that even before the latest trade skirmish, the bank expected some structural damage.
“One thing is clear: the ultimate economic cost of the trade war won’t be measured simply by whether Canada enters a recession,” he said. “Above all, it will depend on what Canadian businesses are still capable of producing years from now.”
Whether the Bank of Canada raises interest rates this month is a “coin toss,” said economists after inflation data Monday.
Canada’s consumer price index breached the bank’s comfort zone of three per cent in September, but the pace was less than economists had expected and core measures remained stable.
However, it was Governor Tiff Macklem’s hawkish comments over the weekend at an IMF meeting in Bangkok that really added doubt to the mix.
Macklem told reporters that given developments in the Iran war the “risk that inflation broadens and becomes more persistent has gone up.”
Robert Kavcic, senior economist for BMO Capital Markets, said in an interview that the central bank will probably raise rates 25 or 50 basis points to get things back to neutral.
“The timing is a bit of a question: Is there enough urgency there for them to go in October?,” he said.

articles.title: Dien Bien province promotes cross-border investment with China, Laos - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: Dien Bien province promotes cross-border investment with China, Laos  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Dien Bien (VNA) – The International Investment Promotion Conference 2026 between Vietnam’s Dien Bien province, China’s Yunnan province and Laos’s Luang Prabang province was held in Dien Bien on October 19, seeking to strengthen economic ties and mobilise resources for socio-economic development.
The conference focused on cooperation in infrastructure, border trade, agricultural product processing, energy and tourism, with investment approvals and cooperation agreements involving tens of trillions of Vietnamese dong announced.
In his opening remarks, Secretary of the Dien Bien Provincial Party Committee Tran Tien Dung emphasised the province’s unique position as Vietnam’s only locality bordering both Laos and China, presenting opportunities to grow into a regional hub for trade, investment, and development cooperation.
Dien Bien also has abundant agricultural and natural resources, historical attractions and distinctive cultural identities. Its economy grew 9.81% in the first nine months of 2026, while 31 projects with registered investment capital exceeding 54 trillion VND (over 2 billion USD) were approved in principle.
The province has identified three priority areas for cooperation, namely transport connectivity, logistics, border trade and processing industries; commercial agriculture and deep processing linked to the green economy; and historical, cultural, ecological and resort tourism.
The official said that Dien Bien hopes to work with Yunnan and Luang Prabang to develop integrated supply and value chains, increase agricultural product value, expand markets and establish internationally attractive tourism routes. It also pledged to streamline administrative procedures, make planning information transparent and improve the business environment.
Vietnamese Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Nguyen Minh Vu called for turning cooperation priorities into feasible projects, with coordinated links between infrastructure, border gates, logistics, production and markets. He stressed that cooperation should facilitate goods circulation, expand business opportunities and create jobs and higher incomes for local residents.
At the conference, investment approval decisions were granted to 20 investors for projects totaling over 7.5 trillion VND in capital. Additionally, memoranda of understanding were exchanged between Dien Bien and six investors, representing nearly 12 trillion VND in registered capital.
The agreements spanned industrial park infrastructure, renewable energy, mineral exploration and processing, urban development, resorts, tourism, trade, services and social housing.
Five secondary investors have also been connected with Thanh An Industrial Park and Thanh Yen 2 Industrial Cluster, with combined registered capital exceeding 2 trillion VND and plans to employ nearly 2,000 local workers. Proposed facilities include agricultural and medicinal herb processing plants, cold storage and post-processing preservation facilities.
The conference also established a cross-border tourism route linking Yunnan, Dien Bien, Laos and Thailand to connect destinations and attract international visitors.
Participants from government agencies, investment promotion organisations and businesses called for better transport, border-gate and logistics connectivity, alongside deeper cooperation in production, investment, processing and cross-border supply chains.
Sun Fenglei, Chairman of the Chinese Business Association in Vietnam, described the conference as an effective platform for connecting authorities and businesses, mobilising resources and advancing practical cooperation. He added that in the coming time, the association will continue bringing reputable Chinese companies to explore investment opportunities and establish long-term operations in Dien Bien.
Lao Ambassador to Vietnam Khamphao Enrthavanh expressed confidence that stronger coordination among local authorities and businesses will expand border trade and translate memoranda of understanding into concrete programmes, projects and contracts, contributing to socio-economic development and improved livelihoods in border areas while strengthening the special friendship between Laos and Vietnam./.

articles.title: Vietnam's export boom offers India six lessons for growth - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Vietnam's export boom offers India six lessons for growth  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Vietnam's success in building an overwhelmingly large export channel is worth examining in India. It's not a story of low wages alone, but also of institutional predictability, tariff simplicity, an extraordinarily wide FTA network, and a state apparatus organised end-to-end around courting and retaining GVC anchors.
India has comparable or larger advantages - market size, engineering talent and capital markets. But it lags on these fronts. Fortunately, this doesn't require reinventing India's economic model but executing at scale on things Vietnam has proven to work. One corrective to the usual argument that Vietnam merely imports from China to export to the West is that Vietnam's exports to China are worth $70 bn. India's are $17-20 bn.
The world is your marketplace
Tariff simplicity Vietnam's simple average applied tariff is around 3.4%, with a trade-weighted average of near 1%. Effective input tariffs for GVC manufacturers are close to zero, and customs classification disputes are rare, because Vietnam has built its tariff and rules-of-origin regime for a small number of high-volume GVC categories rather than the sprawling, exception-laden, litigation-creating schedules in India.
Top-level courtship In August, Vietnam's president To Lam met Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon on the same day its PM Le Minh Hung met Samsung CEO Roh Tae-moon. This signals to a global C-suite that the relationship is a state priority, not a departmental one.
Institutional infra for top exporters Monthly PM office reviews with top exporting GVCs helps policy intent overcome firm-level bottlenecks far faster than an annual budget-cycle, or occasional investor-summit approach. Vietnam's success metric for such investors as being 'net foreign exchange-positive within 10 yrs' should be read as the operating principle officials apply, rather than any published government formula.
Unmatched FTA lattice Vietnam sits inside Asean, RCEP, CPTPP, the EU-Vietnam FTA, and a growing set of bilaterals, giving its exporters near- duty-free access to markets covering the large majority of world GDP, while importing inputs duty-free too.
Scale first, DVA later Vietnam deliberately accepts low domestic value addition (DVA) in the early years of a GVC relationship, targeting only 'net forex-positive within 10 yrs' the same way China did in 2002-15. This is a conscious trade-off against India's more common instinct to gate incentives on local content and value-addition thresholds from year one, which can filter out very high-volume assembly investments that build scale, skills and supplier ecosystems first.
Competitive, predictable tax treatment Zero effective export taxation and a stable corporate tax/incentive regime for GVC investors removes a second layer of negotiation friction that in India often plays out state-by-state and scheme-by-scheme.
Ready for take-off
Move toward a small number of tariff bands for GVC-relevant inputs with pre-published, binding classification rulings. This can be done Asap.
Create a Top 30 Exporters Council chaired at PMO level, paired with state-level counterparts in the 5-6 states that host bulk of India's GVC-scale electronics and auto-components manufacturing, so the engagement is continuous and high-level.
Monthly, not annual, review cadence with these 30 exporting GVCs, with the authority to resolve bottlenecks in real time.
Britain, the EU, EFTA and New Zealand deals are wins on paper. The 3-yr priority is exporter awareness, digitised certificate-of-origin issuance, and rules-of-origin simplification, so utilisation rates approach Vietnam's. India should also quickly conclude a trade deal with the US, still the largest market for Indian goods.
Lower or phase in domestic value-addition thresholds in the first 3-5 yrs of a GVC investment, converging toward Vietnam's 'net-forex-positive in 10 yrs' logic.
Stabilise and simplify the export tax and incentive regime, reducing the degree to which GVC investors must separately negotiate state-level land and power terms on top of central schemes - a single, published national compact that states can opt into.
None of these 6 requires a change in India's economic model. They require sequencing, cadence and predictability, executed with the same diligence and continuity Vietnam has shown for two decades.

articles.title: To help the Vietnamese timber industry escape the situation of "wearing silk robes in the dark" (a metaphor for operating illegally and without proper authorization). - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: To help the Vietnamese timber industry escape the situation of "wearing silk robes in the dark" (a metaphor for operating illegally and without proper authorization).  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Vietnam ranks second in the world for furniture exports, but the majority of the value still lies in the processing stage. To improve its position, the wood industry must learn to master branding and the value chain.
Vietnam's wood industry ranks second in the world for furniture exports, after China . Vietnamese wood products are present in 167 countries and territories. According to information presented at the Trade Promotion Conference, organized by the Trade Promotion Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade) on the afternoon of October 20th, the export value of wood and wood products reached approximately US$17.2 billion. In the first nine months of 2026, this product group brought in about US$13.3-13.43 billion, an increase of 6.3-7.3% compared to the same period last year.
According to Mr. Le Hoang Tai, Deputy Director of the Trade Promotion Department ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ), the above results demonstrate the production capacity, ability to retain customers, and flexibility of businesses in the face of international trade fluctuations.
However, the large export volume of the wood industry does not necessarily translate into a high position in the global value chain. According to Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai, Vice President and General Secretary of the Vietnam Wood and Forest Products Association, the wood industry still relies mainly on two advantages: relatively low labor costs and domestically grown forest raw materials. Meanwhile, many businesses focus on processing orders from foreign importers and distributors under the OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) model. Vietnamese wood products are of good quality but often bear foreign brands when they reach global consumers.
This is the paradoxical situation of the wood industry: "wearing silk in the dark." While production capacity has been recognized internationally, Vietnamese brands, design capabilities, marketing, and distribution haven't kept pace. Businesses create products but haven't fully mastered the stages that determine added value, brand recognition, and direct relationships with end customers.
Dependence on the US market makes this weakness even more apparent. In the first nine months of 2026, the value of indoor and outdoor furniture reached $8.56 billion, remaining almost flat due to declining demand in the US market. Businesses also face tariffs and trade protection measures, along with anti-dumping and anti-subsidy lawsuits against plywood.
Furthermore, geopolitical conflicts, logistical disruptions, and a weakening global market increase costs, putting pressure on production and exports. There is a shortage of large, high-quality domestic timber supplies; capital, compliance, and transportation costs are rising, while small businesses face difficulties in independently developing markets, creating designs, and protecting their brands.
You may also like
"It's not enough to just maintain export growth; we also need to sell products under our own brands and increase the percentage of value retained domestically. Continuing with the old approach will make it difficult to ensure long-term competitiveness in the face of policy changes, demands, and costs in the international market," Mr. Hoai stated.
From outsourcing to owning the brand and value chain.
According to Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai, the goal for Vietnam's wood industry by 2030 is to shift from processing to value creation, aiming for "Made in Vietnam" products designed by Vietnamese people and bearing the "Trusted with Vietnam" brand. To achieve this goal, businesses need to diversify markets, customers, and sales channels, reduce dependence on a single market, and simultaneously upgrade products and build their own brands.
In the United States, businesses need to maintain market share, manage taxes, ensure product origin, and enhance product value. In the EU and the UK, businesses leverage free trade agreements coupled with green standards and traceability. In Japan , businesses focus on quality, reliable delivery, design, and technical materials.
The Netherlands is both a potential market and a logistics hub and distribution gateway to Europe. According to Ms. Vo Thi Ngoc Diep, Vietnam's Trade Counselor in the Netherlands, in the first nine months of 2026, exports of wood and wood products to this market reached US$138 million, an increase of nearly 86% compared to the same period last year.
Dutch consumers prioritize furniture that is simple, multifunctional, space-saving, durable, recyclable, and legally sourced. In the mid-to-high-end segment, custom design, craftsmanship, and quality wood are crucial factors.
To translate potential into orders, businesses must meet increasingly stringent regulations. The European Union's Anti-Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) requires legality, traceability, and geographic location for raw materials within its scope. Therefore, the industry needs to develop legally sourced, traceable raw materials; promote large-scale, high-quality timber plantations; and link production to sustainability standards.
According to Mr. Hoang Trung Thuong, Vietnam's Commercial Counselor in India, populous markets like India and Indonesia offer potential thanks to their young populations and rapid urbanization. However, price competition is fierce. Businesses need to leverage their advantages in design, craftsmanship, and quality; while also researching consumer behavior, legal regulations, safety standards, and labeling in each market.
Combining cross-border e-commerce with direct distribution allows businesses to proactively reach buyers, instead of relying solely on importers.
You may also like
To support businesses, Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai proposed selecting 5-7 priority markets, establishing a focal point for coordination between trade missions and associations; building digital profiles and brand stories; providing trade alerts, connecting with verified buyers, and monitoring opportunities after promotion. Trade promotion activities in 2027 will link trade fairs and business delegations with specific measurable results.
According to Mr. Le Hoang Tai, Deputy Director of the Trade Promotion Department, diversifying markets is not only a solution to find more orders but must also be linked to enhancing product value and competitiveness.
Traditional markets must be strengthened while simultaneously exploring potential markets and selecting segments that match the company's capabilities. This orientation aligns with the Go Global program for the period 2026-2030, which has been approved by the Prime Minister.
