articles.title: Norway and Alaska can tax their resources well, why can't Australia? - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
articles.summary: Norway and Alaska can tax their resources well, why can't Australia?  ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

source_detail.name: ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

articles.full_text:
Does the mineral wealth in our soil and beneath our ocean belong to Australians or to mining companies and their shareholders?
Prosper Australia, a tax reform think tank, says this country has a resource tax and royalty problem.
It estimates Australia is losing $45 billion a year in potential revenue because it is failing to collect more from the extractive mining and gas industries when commodity prices boom and profits surge.
It says we need to fix our tax system's "boom sensitivity" so public revenue rises automatically when public resources generate windfall gains.
"Once coal, iron ore, or gas is extracted and sold, it is gone," the organisation says.
"Companies invest capital, technology, and expertise to extract these resources, and they should earn a commercial return.
"But they do not create the underlying resource, so when resource prices and profits surge, the public should share properly in the upside.
"There is a clear public demand for Australia to rapidly modernise its public-capture mechanisms before more finite public wealth is extracted without a fair public return."
Australia's resource wealth giveaway
The organisation released a report last week, Australia's resource wealth giveaway: How weak public capture leaves billions in revenue on the table.
The report's author was Richard Wielga, a former economist with Victoria's Department of Treasury and Finance.
It compares Australia's resource tax and royalty system against selected resource-rich peers, including Norway, Alaska, Chile, Peru, Québec, and Queensland's coal sector specifically, given Queensland's recent tax changes.
It asks three questions about Australia's resource tax regime:
- Is the system designed to collect more when prices and profits surge?
- What level of revenue does the public actually collect?
- Does stronger public capture automatically drive investment away?
It says if Australia's system had better boom sensitivity, it would collect about $45 billion more every year across state and Commonwealth revenue streams as it rode the global commodity price cycle.
It estimates Australia would collect an extra $28 billion a year from "mining" activity (coal, iron ore, gold, copper, lithium and other miners), and $16—$18 billion from the "petroleum" sector (oil, gas and LNG).
See the graphic below:
International comparisons
The report asks: For every dollar of value created by the resource sector, how much was collected by the public?
It then compares Australia's "public-capture ratio" with some of its global peers.
It shows that Australia's public-capture ratio for petroleum is very weak compared to Norway and Alaska.
It makes the point that Norway's mixed state-participation model is very different to Australia's private-operator model, so to make Norway's public-capture ratio more comparable with Australia's, it removes state-participation activity from Norway's numbers (it makes other adjustments for Alaska).
It shows Australia's mining result is stronger relative to peers, but it could be much stronger, as Queensland coal shows.
"Australia's mining-only public-capture result is stronger than might have been expected," the report says.
"It is higher than the observed ratios for all three selected international mining peers: Quebec, Chile, and Peru.
"That is surprising because Australia's mining design relies heavily on low and flat royalties, while those peers have more boom-sensitive mining regimes.
"[But] this result does not mean Australia's mining royalty design is optimal or that the status quo should remain."
The report says several factors may help to explain the result.
"Actual collection depends on commodity mix, price cycles, project maturity, and cost structures," it says.
"Australia's mining sector includes large, mature, high-volume iron ore and coal production. Quebec, Chile, and Peru have different commodity mixes and cost structures.
"Differences in tax administration and compliance may also affect observed collections."
How different designs respond to a boom differently
The report says not all royalties or taxes respond to resource booms in the same way, and some tax designs can appear good on paper but perform badly.
For example, it says Australia's Petroleum Resource Rent Tax (PRRT) was designed to tax super-profits from offshore petroleum projects, so its boom sensitivity design is high.
But it has failed to produce strong and timely revenues, and current forecasts show no sustained improvement.
"Australia's experience of the PRRT does not mean super-profit taxes cannot work," the report says.
"But it does show that design rules matter and if these are too generous or complex, a resource rent tax can look strong on paper while collecting much less in practice."
Queensland coal is the proof point
The report says recent tax changes in Queensland show that much stronger boom-sensitive public-capture is possible in Australia.
Since July 1, 2022, Queensland's coal royalty scheme has had highly progressive price bands.
Its coal royalty rate rises in several steps with price: from 7 per cent at lower coal prices, to 40 per cent once coal prices exceed $300 a tonne:
- 7 per cent on the first $100/t
- 12.5 per cent on the portion from $100-$150/t
- 15 per cent on the portion from $150-$175/t
- 20 per cent on the portion from $175-$225/t
- 30 per cent on the portion from $225-$300/t
- 40 per cent on the portion above $300/t
Prosper Australia says that kind of royalty schedule is much more "boom-sensitive" than a flat royalty.
Prior to July 1, 2022, the highest Queensland coal rate was 15 per cent on the portion above $150 a tonne.
What happened when the new tax schedule was introduced?
In three years since July 2022, the number of active coal mines in Queensland increased from 53 in 2021–22 to 60 in 2024–25.
The state's coal employment remained around 26,000 workers on a four-quarter average basis, and its saleable coal was "particularly stable", the report says.
Prosper Australia says that evidence is important.
It says arguments have recently been mounting against Queensland's royalty regime, particularly since some mine operators in Queensland began cutting jobs in 2025 and reducing production, blaming higher royalties, alongside falling coal prices and rising costs.
But it says even under a well-designed, boom-sensitive royalty regime, some mines will become uneconomic when global prices fall, costs rise, or deposits mature.
The latest Queensland government figures showed there were 58 active coal mines in Queensland in 2025–26.
Low royalties are a policy choice
Overall, the report makes two suggestions.
It says Australia should modernise its royalties system and address its petroleum under-capture, while allowing viable resource projects to earn a commercial return.
It says governments should adopt market-linked royalties that rise when commodity prices exceed long-run norms.
Or, as an alternative to a purely market-linked royalty, it says states could combine a minimum royalty floor with a second boom-sensitive component linked to prices, profits or profit margins.
"This helps ensure a minimum public return while production continues, and allows the public share to rise when market conditions are strong," it says.
And the same principle should apply when trying to fix Australia's petroleum under-capture, it says.
"This report does not design a new Commonwealth petroleum tax, but future reforms should be judged against the same principle: public returns should rise when prices and profits surge," it says.

articles.title: Supply Chain Resilience: When Supplier Diversification Isn’t Enough - Supply & Demand Chain Executive
articles.summary: Supply Chain Resilience: When Supplier Diversification Isn’t Enough  Supply & Demand Chain Executive
articles.full_text:
Supplier diversification at Tier 1 doesn't guarantee supply chain resilience if those suppliers depend on the same concentrated upstream capabilities, equipment, or materials. True diversification requires identifying independent production pathways and testing whether alternative suppliers can actually function without relying on the same underlying dependencies.
- The diversification gap: Companies often diversify suppliers at Tier 1 while disruption risk remains concentrated in upstream capabilities, equipment, or materials that multiple suppliers share.
- Capability concentration matters more: Three qualified suppliers across different countries may still depend on the same processor, specialized equipment, or technology, creating a single point of failure.
- Geopolitical exposure: Trade restrictions can target not just finished goods but also critical materials, processing technologies, and production equipment used by multiple suppliers.
- Test for independence: Procurement teams should verify how many independent production pathways exist by tracing upstream dependencies, identifying specialized capabilities, and confirming viable alternatives with realistic qualification timelines.
- The real question: Rather than counting suppliers, ask whether an alternative supplier could produce a qualified substitute without relying on the same underlying capability or dependency.
Procurement teams can diversify suppliers without diversifying the production capabilities they depend on. Three qualified suppliers across three countries may still rely on the same processor, specialized equipment, critical material or technical capability.
On a supplier map, the company looks diversified. Several tiers upstream, it may still have one point of failure.
The diversification gap
Supplier diversification has become an important response to geopolitical uncertainty and supply chain disruption. But adding suppliers at Tier 1 does not necessarily eliminate the dependency that created the risk.
KPMG’s 2026 supply chain research identified multi-tier supplier exposure as one of the industry’s leading risks and found that diversification often occurs at Tier 1 while disruption risk remains farther upstream.
The next step is understanding what those suppliers ultimately depend on.
Supplier concentration measures how many companies can provide an input. Capability concentration goes deeper: whether those suppliers depend on the same difficult-to-replace process, equipment, material, technology or expertise.
Three suppliers can still represent one point of failure.
Where the dependency sits
Critical minerals provide a clear example.
The International Energy Agency’s 2026 Global Critical Minerals Outlook found that developing alternative supply requires more than access to another mineral deposit. Diversification can require an ecosystem of processing technology, specialized equipment, technical expertise and skilled workers.
Some of those capabilities remain highly concentrated. The IEA found only a handful of suppliers outside China for certain battery-grade graphite processing equipment. For one rare-earth magnet manufacturing process, it identified only one equipment supplier outside China, with substantially higher costs and longer lead times.
A manufacturer could therefore diversify where it buys a critical component without diversifying the capability required to produce it.
Following the bottleneck
Companies are already putting significant capital behind scarce industrial capabilities.
Precision castings, for example, have been a persistent constraint on engine production, and investment in “mission-critical casting capacity” is necessary to support growing demand across commercial engines, aftermarket and defense.
The bottleneck sits well below the finished aircraft.
Semiconductors show a similar pattern. New fabrication capacity is being built around the world, but advanced production still relies on highly specialized equipment.
Adding factories does not necessarily create independent production pathways when those factories share scarce upstream dependencies.
The geopolitical exposure
This becomes more consequential when capability concentration intersects with geopolitics.
Trade restrictions can reach beyond finished goods to critical materials, components, processing technologies and production equipment. The IEA has documented restrictions extending into technologies and equipment used in critical-mineral processing.
A procurement team could therefore source from suppliers in the United States, Mexico and Europe and still retain exposure to the same concentrated production ecosystem farther upstream.
Geographic diversification at Tier 1 remains valuable. It does not guarantee that the underlying capability has been diversified.
Testing real diversification
For production-critical inputs, procurement teams should look beyond supplier count and ask:
How many qualified suppliers exist? Start with conventional supplier concentration.
Where does production actually occur? Headquarters and manufacturing locations may tell different stories.
Do suppliers share upstream dependencies? Trace common processors, materials and sub-tier suppliers.
What capabilities does production require? Identify specialized equipment, processes, technologies and skills that may be difficult to reproduce.
Does a viable substitute exist? An alternative needs to work technically and commercially.
How long would qualification take? A substitute requiring two years to qualify provides very different resilience from one that can ramp within months.
The objective is not simply to identify another supplier. It is to determine whether that supplier represents a genuinely independent production pathway.
Beyond supplier count
Supply chain visibility is improving. As procurement teams gain better visibility beyond Tier 1, the challenge will be determining which dependencies inside those increasingly detailed maps actually matter.
For every production-critical input, procurement leaders should be able to answer one question:
If this capability became unavailable, could an alternative supplier produce a qualified substitute without relying on the same underlying dependency?
Supplier diversification remains an important resilience strategy. But supplier count alone cannot show whether the underlying means of production have actually been diversified.
Three suppliers can still represent one point of failure. The more important question is how many independent ways a critical product can actually be made.

articles.summary: 2 men rearrested on suspicion of spying for Iran over suspected plot at U.S.-run air base in England  CBS NewsTwo men rearrested on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence service in RAF Fairford incident  CNNTwo men re-arrested on suspicion of assisting Iran intelligence after RAF Fairford incident  BBCThe British Police Rearrest Two in Connection With Alleged Terror Plot  The New York Times2 men rearrested in UK on suspicion of assisting Iran over sus...
articles.full_text:
British police said Tuesday they have rearrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service over the in England last month.
Counter Terrorism Policing said the men, a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old were arrested under the National Security Act.
The men were earlier arrested but had been bailed pending more investigation.
Police are investigating a suspected terror plot on Sept. 27 against the U.S.-run base at RAF Fairford in western England, which has been used to bomb Iran during this year's war.
Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant - gasoline - in three vans at the site, but no explosives.
British authorities have , which led the U.S. to pull its bombers from RAF Fairford.
Five other men who were also arrested earlier remain on bail. No one has yet been charged.
Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the U.K., said detectives are looking at "many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation."
"This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement," he said in a statement.
"Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it," he added.
Iranian officials have said several times since the beginning of the war that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets. But the Iranian Embassy in London said in a previous statement that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.
Earlier this month, the U.S. Air Force all of its bombers from the air base following the security incident.

articles.title: Egypt moves toward sending troops to Saudi Arabia to help defend against attacks by Iran-backed Houthis - CBS News
articles.summary: Egypt moves toward sending troops to Saudi Arabia to help defend against attacks by Iran-backed Houthis  CBS NewsEgyptian Lawmakers Push Back on Sisi’s Request to Send Troops to Saudi Arabia  الحرةExplainer: What's behind Egypt's move towards possible military involvement in Saudi-Yemen conflict?  ReutersWhat help can Egypt offer Saudi Arabia in the war against the Houthis?  Al JazeeraEgypt Is Inactive No More  Geopolitical Futures
articles.full_text:
Cairo - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has asked the country's Parliament to authorize the military to help defend Saudi Arabia after Yemen's intensified their attacks on the kingdom, targeting and oil infrastructure.
Al-Sisi stressed that it would be a defensive mission and only if the kingdom requests assistance.
"Egypt will take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to protect and defend it," al-Sisi said Saturday during a military graduation ceremony.
Under Egypt's Constitution, the president must consult the National Defense Council and obtain approval from two-thirds of Parliament before deploying the armed forces on a combat mission abroad.
On Sunday, al-Sisi chaired a meeting of the National Defense Council, which reviewed what the Egyptian presidency described as the "grave escalations unfolding in the region" and the "unacceptable attacks" against Saudi Arabia.
The council pledged to provide "all necessary and possible forms of support to the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to defend its security and stability, and to safeguard its resources, territorial integrity, and Islamic holy sites."
Egypt has managed, so far, to stay out of all the recent military conflicts in the region and has tried to de-escalate and find political solutions. For some, this is one of al-Sisi's greatest achievements.
But Samir Ragheb, a retired army brigadier and political and strategic analyst, told CBS News that it was time for Egypt to make good on commitments it had made to helping secure the region.
"Egypt has repeatedly pledged to support the security of the Gulf states and has issued numerous statements reaffirming this commitment," Ragheb said. "However, this is a time of war, not politics and statements. If Egypt fails to deliver on these promises, they will lose their meaning and amount to nothing more than empty threats."
"The Gulf states have invested billions of dollars in Egypt. Morally, it's Egypt's turn to return the favor," he said.
Parliament convened an emergency session on Sunday and was expected to approve the resolution on Tuesday, but the vote was postponed until next Monday.
The Egyptian Social Democratic Party instructed its parliamentary bloc to abstain from voting on the resolution, saying in a statement it had not received sufficient information about "the mission's scope, costs, and risks, as well as the arrangements in place to protect Egyptian forces."
Ragheb is certain the region is heading toward a more severe escalation.
"Egypt is not going to defend the kingdom against the Houthis," he said. "The threat is much bigger than the Houthis. This includes Iran, Iraqi militias and sleeper cells within the kingdom itself."
However, he also believes Egypt will lose much of its influence in the region if it doesn't intervene.
"If you want to be a regional player, you must play a role," he said. "Otherwise, you will lose your seat at the table."
Ragheb argued that the United States' in support of Saudi Arabia created a vacuum that must be filled by others. He said Egypt should take on the Arab share of that role.
Other regional powers are also trying to fill the vacuum. In August, Saudi Arabia signed a joint defense agreement with Turkey and Pakistan known as the Mecca Accords.
"Even before Saudi Arabia asked for Egyptian support, the Mecca Accords was a death certificate for the idea of relying on America for any form of defense," Ragheb said.

articles.title: Nothing significant will happen in country's industrial sector without proper planning - Prothom Alo English
articles.summary: Nothing significant will happen in country's industrial sector without proper planning  Prothom Alo English
articles.full_text:
Last month, you submitted a proposal to the Ministry of Commerce to open branches of Chinese banks in Bangladesh. Why have you suddenly taken the initiative to bring Chinese banks to the country?
Khorshed Alam: China is our largest trading partner. Annual trade between the two countries exceeds $20 billion. Even countries like Sri Lanka have a bank in Bangladesh — the Bank of Ceylon. We import so many products from China that having a Chinese bank here would offer several advantages. It would reduce the costs of imports and exports.
Could you explain how bilateral trade would benefit once Chinese banks begin operations?
Khorshed Alam: Suppose we export goods worth around $700 million to China. If this amount is deposited in our bank accounts in China's currency, the yuan, we could use those funds to import goods from China. In that case, there would be no need to settle import and export payments in US dollars or convert dollars into yuan or taka. This would reduce intermediary bank commissions and currency conversion costs. On average, it could save us around 1 per cent of the total amount. In these difficult times, even a 1 per cent saving is significant.
Another issue is that many of our banks lack capital and are unable to provide working capital. Chinese banks, if they enter the market, will certainly bring in capital. They will not simply bring in money and leave it idle. To operate a bank, they will have to invest that money, provide loans and make profits. Some of our industrial enterprises could potentially access capital from these banks. This is precisely why we are proposing the introduction of Chinese banks.
China is now Bangladesh’s second-largest source of foreign investment. Last year, China’s net FDI reached its highest level in six years. What types of industries are Chinese investors currently interested in?
Khorshed Alam: Chinese economic zones are being developed in Anwara, Chattogram, and Mongla, Bagerhat. According to Invest Bangladesh, formerly the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (BIDA), Chinese investment in Anwara could reach $1.3 billion. However, construction of the economic zone's infrastructure is expected to be completed in 2031.
The Chinese are primarily interested in investing in the textile and leather sectors. In textiles, they are particularly interested in fabric production. Bangladesh’s large domestic market and opportunities for garment exports are attracting them to invest more in this sector.
Another promising area is producing fibre from garment industry waste. Some Chinese companies are buying garment waste, commonly known as jhut, from Bangladesh, processing it into fibre and exporting it to Vietnam. The fibre is then used to produce yarn and sweaters. If this type of activity can be carried out in Bangladesh, value can be added locally.
Besides, they are also showing interest in manufacturing lithium batteries, solar power equipment and hospital equipment. In particular, discussions are underway about investment in lithium battery manufacturing.
Due to high tariffs, many Chinese products are facing barriers to exports to the US market. If Chinese companies bring their technology to Bangladesh and manufacture those products here as ‘Made in Bangladesh’ goods, exports could grow rapidly. This is because they already have established markets. I believe such an arrangement would be beneficial for Bangladesh.
China is far ahead in terms of technology. Can’t we attract investment from China in high-tech industries in the Anwara and Mongla economic zones?
Khorshed Alam: We should certainly make that effort. However, the problem is that there is a shortage of skilled manpower for high-tech industries in the country. To address this shortage, polytechnic institutes should be established near the economic zones. This would allow the Chinese to develop a workforce with the skills they require.
Another important issue is that workers’ residential quarters must be built near the economic zones. There are hardly any houses around Anwara, so workers would have to be brought from 30–40 miles away. This would be quite expensive. In addition, facilities such as schools, hospitals and markets must also be ensured.
Does the government have any guidelines on what types of investment we want from China?
Khorshed Alam: It is better to identify specific sectors for foreign investment. Suppose a Chinese entrepreneur says, “I want to set up a spinning mill,” we should then ask why. If the entrepreneur says they want to sell yarn in the local market, we should tell them that we do not need this investment. But if a Chinese entrepreneur says they want to export the products to Vietnam, China or South Korea, then that is fine.
Besides, if Chinese entrepreneurs want to manufacture lithium batteries, they should be welcomed. They should also be given quick approval if they want to manufacture solar panels. We need investment in these sectors. Chinese entrepreneurs should also be welcomed if they want to manufacture battery-powered motorcycles or cars.
Is there an opportunity to attract Chinese investment to Bangladesh and export the products manufactured here to China?
Khorshed Alam: Small factories are currently shutting down in China. They no longer want to manufacture simple items such as ballpoint pens. They are not interested in making ceramic cups or small products such as plastic bottles either. They want to manufacture high-tech products, such as mobile phones, which have higher prices.
As a result, it is possible to manufacture products in Bangladesh that are in demand in China and export them there. This can also be achieved through Chinese investment.
For example, China imports 30 per cent of its demand for readymade garments from around the world. Although large quantities of readymade garments are exported to China from Vietnam, Indonesia and Thailand, Bangladesh exports very little to that market. There is an opportunity to increase Bangladesh's garment exports to China.
To facilitate duty-free sales of Bangladeshi products in the Chinese market, Bangladesh is set to receive a permanent exhibition centre and a warehouse free of charge in Kunming. We can display Bangladeshi products there and increase exports.
What are the major obstacles faced by Chinese investors when investing in Bangladesh?
Khorshed Alam: The biggest complaint from Chinese investors at the moment is the energy crisis. They are asking how they can invest if they cannot get energy. Second, the shortage of technically skilled workers is also a concern for them.
Besides, they have some uncertainty over whether they will have access to banking facilities. They are also concerned about security and extortion.
One of our members recently brought a complaint to me. Someone had demanded extortion money from a battery manufacturing factory in Madhabdi, Narsingdi. However, the businessman is afraid to file a formal complaint.
Vietnam has transformed its industrial sector by attracting investment from South Korea’s Samsung. Is there an opportunity to attract similar investment from China that could bring about a major transformation in our industrial sector?
Khorshed Alam: We lack the planning needed to bring about major changes. The Mongla Economic Zone, which was recently handed over to China, was initially allocated to India.
After waiting for a decade, the foundation stone of the Chinese Economic Zone in Anwara was laid last July. So, why was the land left unused for so long? No output was generated despite leaving the land unused for so many years.
Therefore, I believe nothing significant will happen in the country's industrial sector without proper planning.
How can we develop a skilled workforce like China's?
Khorshed Alam: We have a promising young generation in our country. There is an opportunity to equip this generation with technical skills. We can then use those skills to make our industries much more competitive.
At the same time, we must develop a skilled workforce to operate high-tech industries. To achieve this, we need to learn how China has used technology to reduce production costs. We should bring in Chinese experts if necessary. I believe this is how we can accelerate the development of our national economy.

articles.title: 5 priority actions to enhance the position of Vietnamese wood and increase export value. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: 5 priority actions to enhance the position of Vietnamese wood and increase export value.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Large potential but increasing competitive pressure.
 In 2025, exports of wood and wood products are expected to reach approximately $17.2 billion. In the first nine months of 2026, this figure is projected to reach approximately $13.43 billion, a 6.3% increase compared to the same period of the previous year.
 At the trade promotion briefing conference in October 2026, held on the afternoon of October 20th with the theme "Diversifying markets, promoting the export of Vietnamese wood and furniture products," Mr. Phung Quoc Man, Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City Handicraft and Wood Processing Association (HAWA), stated that Vietnamese wood products are present in 167 countries and territories. Vietnam currently ranks second in the world for furniture exports, after China , with a diverse supply capacity ranging from home, office, and outdoor furniture to products for construction projects and hotels.
 According to Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai, Vice President and General Secretary of the Vietnam Wood and Forest Products Association, the wood industry has formed a relatively complete ecosystem from forest planting, harvesting, processing to export. There are approximately 6,000 businesses operating in the industry nationwide, of which more than 3,500 focus on exports, including over 700 foreign-invested enterprises (FDI).
 However, the industry remains heavily reliant on the US market, which typically accounts for over 50% of export revenue. Tariff policies and trade protection measures in this market are putting pressure on businesses. High logistics costs, traceability requirements, and regulations on preventing forest degradation also pose increasing challenges. 
 Mr. Le Hoang Tai, Deputy Director of the Trade Promotion Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade), believes that diversifying markets is not only about seeking more orders but also about enhancing product value and competitiveness. Businesses need to consolidate traditional markets, exploit potential markets, and at the same time understand customer needs, import conditions, and appropriate access channels.
 Several markets are opening up notable opportunities. In the Netherlands , in the first nine months of 2026, Vietnam's exports of wood and wood products reached US$138 million, an 86% increase compared to the same period the previous year. The Netherlands is also a logistics and distribution hub for goods entering the EU. Meanwhile, the Indian furniture market is estimated to be worth approximately US$22 billion, projected to reach US$30-40 billion in the near future, with an average annual growth rate of 8-10%.
 However, according to Mr. Bui Trung Thuong, Vietnam's Commercial Counselor in India , India is also a difficult market to access due to protectionist policies for domestic production and technical barriers. The most-favored-nation import duty on furniture is 20%, while goods from countries with free trade agreements with India, including ASEAN, enjoy a duty rate of 0-5%. Businesses also need to be aware of trade defense measures and certification requirements from the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS). 
 Mr. Bui Trung Thuong - Commercial Counselor of Vietnam in India. (Screenshot)
 Five priorities to elevate the status of Vietnamese wood.
 To enhance his position in the global value chain, Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai proposed five priority actions.
 Firstly, diversify markets, customers, and sales channels, reducing dependence on a single market. In the US, businesses need to maintain market share, manage tariff and origin risks, and seek new markets, including niche markets. In the EU and UK, they should leverage free trade agreements; in Japan and South Korea , they should expand opportunities for interior and exterior products. Businesses should also explore potential in the Middle East, ASEAN, Australia, and other markets.
 Secondly, investing in design, technology, artificial intelligence (AI), productivity, and human resource skills will gradually shift from contract manufacturing to proactively developing products and owning the brand.
 Thirdly, developing large-timber plantations ensures the legality and traceability of raw materials, meeting the increasingly high demands of importing markets.
 Fourth, build the brand of Vietnamese wood and furniture, and develop direct distribution channels to enhance the value that businesses receive from exported products.
 Fifth, harmoniously link product groups from wood chips, pellets, wood panels to furniture, thereby increasing the value obtained per cubic meter of wood.
 According to Mr. Hoai, the industry needs to shift from purely OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) to ODM (Original Design Manufacturer), aiming for brand ownership. The goal is to create "Made in Vietnam" products, designed by Vietnamese people, bearing Vietnamese brands, and trusted by international customers. 
 Mr. Phung Quoc Man - Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City Handicraft and Wood Processing Association (HAWA). (Screenshot)  To achieve these priorities, the supportive role of the Vietnamese trade office system abroad is crucial. Mr. Phung Quoc Man suggested that trade offices provide focused information on market needs, customer segments, distribution channels, and import requirements; verify partners; connect businesses with importers and retailers; and monitor the cooperation process from sample submission and quotation to negotiation and order signing.
 Associations and businesses also need to coordinate closely with the Trade Promotion and Business Office to promote production capabilities, attract international buyers to Vietnam to attend specialized trade fairs and exhibitions, and conduct factory surveys.
 According to Mr. Le Hoang Tai, market diversification needs to go hand in hand with enhancing competitiveness and participating more deeply in the value-creating stages of the supply chain. This is also a direction consistent with the "Go Global" program for the period 2026–2030, approved by Decision No. 626/QD-TTg dated June 4, 2026.
 The ultimate goal is not only to bring more wood products to the international market, but also to help Vietnamese brands become more clearly recognized, enabling businesses to be more proactive in the value chain and benefit proportionally to their production capacity.
 Nguyet Minh

articles.title: Aito shifts from Huawei to Bosch for European expansion - CarNewsChina.com
articles.summary: Aito shifts from Huawei to Bosch for European expansion  CarNewsChina.com
articles.full_text:
At the 2026 Paris Motor Show, Seres, the manufacturer of the Huawei-backed brand Aito, officially announced that Aito is set to enter the European market in the autumn of 2027.
To facilitate this global expansion, Aito is adopting a “Bosch Inside” partnership model for its overseas lineup. According to industry insiders quoted by 36kr, the international versions of the Aito 6, 7, 8, and 9 will be developed in collaboration with the global automotive giant Bosch. These vehicles will feature a suite of Bosch’s intelligent technologies, covering advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS), intelligent cockpits, and chassis systems.
Development for these overseas models is already underway, with plans to mass-produce high-speed Navigate on Autopilot (NOA) capabilities by September of next year.
While Aito has achieved success in China through its deep collaboration with Huawei, sources indicate that for the overseas market, Seres Group has taken the lead in decision-making. The “Bosch Inside” model is described by those close to the project as being conceptually similar to Huawei’s “Huawei Inside” (HI) model, leveraging the international expertise and regulatory familiarity of a global partner to navigate the complexities of the European market.
Global competition
The push into Europe comes as Chinese automakers face intensifying competition and cost pressures in their home market. With domestic retail sales experiencing a downward trend, brands are increasingly looking to overseas markets to establish new growth engines.
Aito’s entry into Europe follows previous attempts by other high-end Chinese brands, such as Nio, which faced challenges in the region due to brand recognition and the complexities of establishing sales and service networks. To ensure a smoother transition, Seres has reportedly integrated its overseas business unit into the Aito Business Group, streamlining the coordination of research, development, and market strategy.

articles.title: Diversifying markets and boosting exports of Vietnamese wood and furniture. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Diversifying markets and boosting exports of Vietnamese wood and furniture.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
On the afternoon of October 20th, in Hanoi, the Trade Promotion Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade) organized a trade promotion meeting with the system of Vietnamese trade offices abroad for October 2026, with the theme "Diversifying markets, promoting the export of Vietnamese wood and furniture products," using a hybrid format combining in-person and online participation.
The conference focused on evaluating export results, identifying challenges in major markets, and proposing solutions to expand markets and strengthen trade connections for businesses in the wood and furniture industry.
In his opening remarks at the conference, Mr. Le Hoang Tai stated: In 2025, Vietnam's exports of wood and wood products are expected to reach approximately US$17.2 billion, continuing to play a crucial role in the country's overall export structure. In the first nine months of 2026, export turnover for this product group is estimated to reach US$13.43 billion, an increase of 7.3% compared to the same period last year.
According to Mr. Le Hoang Tai, the above results reflect the efforts of the business community to maintain production, seek orders, and adapt to market fluctuations. However, the wood and furniture industry still faces many challenges from trade policies, tariffs, and trade protection measures in major markets. Therefore, along with maintaining growth momentum, businesses need to enhance their resilience and proactively respond to changes in the international business environment.
"Businesses need to proactively manage origin, ensure the source of raw materials, and meet the requirements of each market right from the production stage," Mr. Le Hoang Tai emphasized, adding that diversifying markets should not only focus on finding more orders but also on enhancing product value and competitiveness.
Based on this, in addition to consolidating traditional markets, businesses need to proactively explore markets with significant potential, selecting segments that match their production capacity and customer requirements. Market expansion should also go hand in hand with research into consumer demand, import conditions, technical standards, design trends, and distribution systems in each locality.
This provides a basis for businesses to adjust products, develop brands, and enhance their ability to participate in value-creating stages of the supply chain, in line with the orientation of the Go Global Program for the period 2026–2030, which has been approved by the Prime Minister .
To support businesses in effectively implementing these directions, Mr. Le Hoang Tai suggested that the system of Vietnamese trade offices abroad strengthen the provision of market information in a specific and practical manner. This includes clarifying promising product groups, customer segments, design trends, distribution channels, and the ability to access partners in each market; and promptly updating changes in tariffs, technical standards, traceability, and trade defense measures, helping businesses proactively prepare documentation and meet the regulations of importing countries.
You may also like
Along with providing information, strengthening coordination between trade missions, industry associations, and businesses is identified as a crucial solution to enhance the effectiveness of trade promotion. Associations and businesses need to share the difficulties they face in finding customers, developing products, meeting standards, and organizing promotional activities so that trade missions have a basis for building appropriate support programs. Networking activities should be prepared early, based on the specific needs of businesses, and followed up after connection, aiming to form cooperative relationships and secure substantial orders.
Assessing the industry's position, Mr. Phung Quoc Man, Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City Handicraft and Wood Processing Association (HAWA), stated: Vietnam currently ranks second in the world in furniture exports, after China ; Vietnamese wood products are present in 167 countries and territories. "This position is built on production capacity, craftsmanship, and the ability to meet the stringent requirements of international customers," Mr. Phung Quoc Man affirmed.
Vietnamese businesses have the capacity to supply a diverse range of products, from home, office, and outdoor furniture to products for construction projects and hotels; while continuing to invest in design, technology, management, and legally sourced, sustainable raw materials.
To build upon that foundation, according to Mr. Phung Quoc Man, the wood industry needs to consolidate traditional markets and expand into markets with remaining potential. The support of the trade delegation system is of practical significance, helping businesses understand the market, access partners, and develop orders.
According to Mr. Phung Quoc Man, the wood industry has recently received information from trade missions in the UAE, India , Mexico, Kuwait, and Pakistan regarding buyers interested in Vietnam seeking wood processing factories. These connections indicate a significant demand for orders, expanded production cooperation, and supplier placements in Vietnam. Therefore, this is an opportunity to showcase the industry's capabilities and coordinate efforts to transform these real needs into cooperation opportunities and orders for businesses.
In 2027, the wood and furniture industry will continue to organize trade fairs and exhibitions in Vietnam, including: HawaExpo 2027 - Ho Chi Minh City Wood and Furniture Export Fair; VIBE 2027 - Vietnam Furniture and Construction Exhibition connecting furniture with architecture, construction, materials and design.
“The wood and furniture industry trade fairs and exhibitions held recently have created a buzz, contributing to promoting Vietnamese businesses. This is an effective form of on-site export promotion, allowing customers to directly view products, work with suppliers, and combine factory tours in a single trip,” Mr. Phung Quoc Man affirmed.
The Chairman of HAWA hopes that the Trade Offices will pay attention to introducing these programs to import associations, distribution systems, and buyers in their respective areas, bringing more international customers to learn about and cooperate with Vietnamese businesses. He also hopes that after the workshop, the parties will identify coordination points, priority markets, and specific activities to implement together, making the cooperation between the Trade Promotion Department, trade offices, associations, and businesses increasingly frequent and practical.
You may also like
The October 2026 trade promotion briefing conference was held with two working sessions, focusing on diversifying markets and promoting trade connections for Vietnam's wood and furniture industry.
Accordingly, delegates focused on discussing the results of Vietnam's wood and furniture exports in the first nine months of 2026; the impact of tariff policies and trade defense measures in major markets; and proposed solutions to diversify markets and reduce dependence on a few traditional markets. In addition, discussions focused on opportunities for expanding exports, import requirements, and consumption potential in key markets such as India, the Netherlands , Spain, the UAE, and Australia.
Furthermore, delegates also emphasized the role of specialized trade fairs and exhibitions in promoting production and design capabilities, connecting businesses with international buyers; and discussed solutions to strengthen coordination between the Vietnamese trade office system abroad and businesses in providing market information, removing trade barriers, and promoting the export of wood and furniture products.
Through direct exchanges between trade promotion agencies, trade offices, associations, and businesses, the conference aims to enhance access to information, accurately identify market needs, and improve the effectiveness of partner connections. This will provide the Vietnamese wood and furniture industry with a stronger foundation to diversify markets, proactively address trade barriers, and better exploit export opportunities in the future.

The Trade Promotion Department will compile the recommendations and coordinate with the Trade Offices system, relevant agencies, and industry associations to integrate them into the work plan. articles.title: Irish technology exports surge 141% despite overall trade decline - IrishCentral
articles.summary: Irish technology exports surge 141% despite overall trade decline  IrishCentral
articles.full_text:
Exports of the technology-related products reached €1.4bn in August, up from €587.8m in the same month last year. However, the figure was down from €2.3bn recorded in July.
Total Irish exports fell by €184.7m, or 1.2%, to €15.9bn in August 2026 compared with August 2025, while imports of office machinery and automatic data processing equipment rose by 63.4% to €2bn.
The increase in technology-related trade comes amid continued international investment in artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure, highlighting Ireland’s role in global technology and advanced manufacturing supply chains.
However, exports of medical and pharmaceutical products declined by 6.7% year-on-year to €6bn, while organic chemical exports fell by 28.6% to €1.5bn.
Pharmaceutical products remain a major contributor to Irish exports, although the latest figures point to further moderation following the exceptionally high levels recorded during 2025.
Lorna Kelly, director of BDO Customs and International Trade Services, said the figures reinforced the importance of efficient customs procedures and reliable access to international markets.
“For businesses operating in the technology and pharmaceutical sectors, this reinforces the importance of maintaining efficient customs procedures, accurate classification and reliable access to international markets, particularly as trade restrictions and regulatory requirements continue to evolve,” she said.
Read more
Kelly also highlighted changing trade patterns within the semiconductor industry, particularly Ireland’s relationship with China.
Irish semiconductor exports to China have declined considerably in recent years, while alternative Asian markets, including Malaysia, have become increasingly important destinations.
Kelly said the shift highlighted the potential influence of international export controls, changing manufacturing arrangements and geopolitical developments on global technology supply chains.
She added that market diversification remained important as Irish exporters responded to changes in international trade policy.
Seasonally adjusted exports declined by 7.1% compared with July, while Ireland’s trade surplus narrowed to €2.6bn.
“Overall, the August figures demonstrate the importance of looking beyond headline export performance,” Kelly said, adding that continued annual growth in technology-related trade represented a more positive underlying development.

articles.title: The more big companies axe staff, the closer we get to a recession - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
articles.summary: The more big companies axe staff, the closer we get to a recession  ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

source_detail.name: ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

articles.full_text:
You won't find NAB employees exiting their offices in Sydney and Melbourne carrying cardboard boxes with small ferns sticking out the top.
There's been no major financial or economic shock, notwithstanding ongoing oil market turmoil.
Instead, NAB's cold and brutal axing of 2,500 staff, announced this week, is a calculated move to make one of Australia's biggest companies nimbler.
"Our ambition and strategy remain unchanged," NAB Group chief executive Andrew Irvine said.
"We will improve productivity, risk outcomes and execution to be a simpler and more efficient bank."
It's not alone.
Late last year ANZ flagged a reduction in "duplication and internal complexity" as part of its own organisational restructure and, as NAB said on Tuesday, that there would be limited impact on frontline, customer-facing roles.
If the Commonwealth Bank and Westpac follow suit, along with other large non-bank corporations letting staff go, we might have a major problem.
Economic head winds
Australia's big four banks are operating in a challenging economic environment and, they insist, need to adapt.
The root of their problems comes from Australia's astounding inability to generate reasonable levels of productivity growth.
Productivity (as measured by the ABS as GDP per hour worked) was -0.2 per cent in the 12 months to June.
This means the national economy can only grow so fast before generating inflation, because businesses struggle to absorb the costs of production and so need to pass those costs onto customers when they demand goods and services.
Add to this an oil price shock, and the Reserve Bank has been forced to hike interest rates four times this year to tame inflation.
The Commonwealth Bank's chief economist Luke Yeaman says, in a worst-case scenario, the RBA may need to hike interest rates on Melbourne Cup Day, and again early next year.
"If you look at these structural factors, we've got a historic AI boom coming through the system, driving up inflation, driving up costs," Mr Yeaman said.
"You've got still strong government spending; you've got low productivity, and rising neutral interest rates around the world.
"So you put all that together and actually inflation might be much more persistent and the RBA may have to continue hiking rates through this year and even into early next year."
Cost crunch
It means the big four banks are being financially squeezed.
Money is seeping out of the housing market, for example.
The total number of new loan commitments for dwellings, according to the ABS's June quarter lending indicators report, fell 5.4 per cent.
The number of new investor loan commitments for dwellings fell 8.6 per cent in the quarter.
The bank's net interest margins or, very loosely speaking, the margin between the interest rate they pay depositors and the rates they charge borrowers, is also coming under pressure as interest rates rise.
Meanwhile, their combined profit after tax was $15.2 billion, down by 2.1 per cent compared to the first half.
Enter the lure of outsourcing roles offshore and rolling out artificial intelligence (AI), and you have several vehicles at management's disposal to cut costs in the face of weakening revenue.
There were no specific references to any of this in the NAB's public statements today, though.
"We are particularly focused on reducing the size of corporate functions," Andrew Irvine said.
"There will be no material impact to customer-facing banking roles.
"We have also deliberately made deeper changes to senior management positions which will broaden leadership responsibilities across the bank," he said.
Nimbler? Yes. How will this be achieved? That's harder to say.
More economic and business analysis
Biting the hand that feeds you
Section 181 of the Corporations Act 2001 requires directors to "exercise their powers and discharge their duties: in good faith in the best interests of the corporation; and for a proper purpose".
The final report of the Royal Commission into Misconduct in the Banking, Superannuation and Financial Services Industry was submitted by Commissioner Kenneth Hayne who noted, "self-interest will almost always trump duty".
This was a reference to chasing profits for a company ahead of the best interests of the client.
For banks, at the very top levels, it's a painfully simple maths problem: grow revenue and cut costs.
It boosts the banks' bottom lines, which grows shareholder value and, in turn, lines the pockets of executives.
But is that too short sighted?
Those who have been let go from ANZ Bank and those about to be let go from NAB are facing a deteriorating jobs market, and rising interest rates.
If CBA and Westpac follow suit, it could be a real problem for the economy.
Because it's not just the banks letting go of workers.
Mining giant BHP last week confirmed job cuts at its iron ore operations in Western Australia.
And Microsoft announced it would cut 4,800 jobs, or about 2.1 per cent of its global workforce, in July.
The Reserve Bank wants to reduce "aggregate demand" in the economy to help lower inflation.
Governor Michele Bullock said it might take an unemployment rate of 5 per cent to achieve that.
You can see now, though, why Bullock could "possibly" see a recession in sight, given how many companies may choose to become "more agile" as times get tougher.
The negative feedback loop in the economy is plain to see: more job losses feed more job losses.
What is less clear is how much further interest rates can rise before that feedback loop is turbo-charged — though some in finance have a view on it.
ABC business editor Michael Janda asked panellists at the Citi Investment Conference in Sydney today how much further the RBA could raise interest rates before bigger cracks appeared in the mortgage market, with rising arrears and forced sales.
"I don't think it's a lot more," said James Boyle, the chief executive of major non-bank lender Liberty Financial Group.
"There's an increase in hardship … borrowers are doing it tough with rates at the current levels."
He added: "The stress is there if you go looking for it."
David Bailey, chief executive of large mortgage broking group AFG, agreed, saying inflation and falling real wages had eroded many borrowers' financial buffers.
"The cost of living has increased at the same time … that causes real cracks to start to appear," he warned.
"An extra 25 [basis points] is really starting to push the envelope."
Former NAB chief economist Alan Oster said, all else being equal, Australia would hit an unemployment rate of 4.8 per cent by early next year.
If the RBA hikes interest rates again, he said, it will move higher to 5 per cent. He characterised that as a recession.
With gross federal government debt of roughly $1 trillion, business confidence in the doldrums and weak productivity, the economy is in a particularly vulnerable position to handle a corporate Australia race to the bottom in cutting costs.

articles.title: Malaysia's export boom lifts 2026 growth outlook, AI demand provides support - Malaysia Sun
articles.summary: Malaysia's export boom lifts 2026 growth outlook, AI demand provides support  Malaysia Sun
articles.full_text:
Xinhua
                
20 Oct 2026, 12:45 GMT+10
            
KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia's export growth outlook for 2026 has strengthened on robust demand for semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and electrical and electronics (E&E) products, prompting research houses to raise their forecasts, although external uncertainties and fading base effects could temper trade momentum towards year-end.
RHB Investment Bank Research said in a note on Monday that it has raised its forecast for Malaysia's export growth in 2026 to 34.4 percent from 21.7 percent, following a robust 34 percent expansion year to date, supported by strong demand for E&E products.
E&E exports, a key driver of the strong performance, are expected to remain resilient for the rest of the year, while commodity-related exports, particularly liquefied natural gas (LNG) and petroleum products, should provide additional support, the research house said.
RHB said it remained watchful of uncertainties surrounding the sustainability of the AI investment cycle, geopolitical developments and U.S. tariff policies, which could affect global demand and trade flows.
However, Malaysia's diversified economic base, deep integration into global and regional supply chains, and efforts to diversify export markets and broaden its product mix should help sustain export growth and cushion external headwinds.
Separately, MBSB Research has upgraded its 2026 export growth forecast to 32 percent, from 6.6 percent growth in 2025, while raising its import growth projection to 26 percent, compared with 6 percent last year.
Sustained demand for E&E and technology-related products should support exports, alongside stronger imports of inputs for manufacturing and investment activities, it said.
BIMB Securities said robust external demand, particularly for AI and electronics, suggested Malaysia's growth momentum could be stronger than initially estimated.
Strong demand for semiconductors, AI infrastructure and data centers continues to support manufacturing, the research house said, adding that the AI upcycle should underpin healthy economic expansion even as growth moderates in 2027.

articles.title: Australia's economy is growing, so why do we all feel poorer? - Money magazine
articles.summary: Australia's economy is growing, so why do we all feel poorer?  Money magazine
articles.full_text:
Australia's economy grew 2.1% over the past year, unemployment remains low and the country has avoided recession. Yet many Australians feel worse off than they did five years ago.
For many households, the explanation is simple: prices have risen faster than incomes. While the economy has continued to grow, higher living costs and interest rates have left many Australians feeling poorer despite positive headline economic figures.
So why is there such a gap between the economic data and everyday reality?
How is the Australian economy performing?
On paper, Australia's economy is doing pretty well.
Australia's GDP grew by 2.1% between June 2025 and June 2026, which is a decent growth rate considering other developed countries like the UK grew at 1.2% and the US at 2.2% in the same period. The latest growth rate was also above what markets and analysts had expected.
Another economic indicator, the unemployment rate, was low at 4.7% in September 2026, meaning most people who want a job are able to find one.
Considering the conflict in the Middle East is still pushing up oil prices, causing input costs to increase for Australian businesses, and the impacts of artificial intelligence on the workforce remain uncertain, the economy isn't doing too badly at all.
In September, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) also increased the cash rate, which acts as a brake to slow down the economy, to 4.6%, the highest it has been in 15 years.
The board expressed some concerns about inflation pressures, but noted economic growth had been stronger than anticipated.
Why are people so pessimistic about the economy?
For many households, the issue is simple: prices have risen faster than incomes, making it harder for people to get ahead even while the economy grows.
Most Australians are earning less money in real terms than they were five years ago, contributing to a general pessimism about the state of the economy. The inflation rate has averaged around 4.4% annually over the past five years, while annual wage growth has averaged about 3.4%, with some fluctuations.
A 2026 report from the OECD, a group of mostly developed countries, noted that Australia had some of the weakest real wage recovery since the start of the cost-of-living crisis.
In other words, many Australians are still spending more on essentials such as groceries, fuel and housing than they were a few years ago, without seeing equivalent gains in their pay packets.
Behavioural economist Phil Slade said people don't experience the economy through headline indicators like GDP growth. Instead, they judge it through the costs they encounter every day.
"They experience the petrol bowser, the mortgage statement and the weekly shop. When fuel is back above $2.30 a litre and the cash rate is at its highest since 2011, those reminders are hitting people several times a week, and that adds up to a constant low hum of stress," he says.
What is a recession, and is Australia in one?
Despite widespread cost-of-living pressures, Australia is not officially in recession.
The most common definition of a recession, called a "technical recession", is two consecutive quarters of negative growth in real GDP.
By this definition, Australia has not recorded a recession since the early 1990s.
However, this official indicator can hide slow GDP growth and can be influenced by volatile changes in some sectors of the economy. For example, the national GDP figure can grow because of an increase in the number of migrants working in the country.
For this reason, some experts prefer to use GDP growth per capita to measure how the economy is going. Others may use increases in the unemployment rate to identify a recession.
Is GDP growth still the best measure of economic health?
It depends on what exactly you're trying to measure.
For the RBA, commercial banks, investors and policymakers, GDP growth shows the health of the economy as a whole. GDP growth numbers broken down by sector, such as mining, agriculture or retail, can also give a better idea of how and where the economy is growing or declining.
However, if you're trying to understand how households are coping, it can be more useful to look at spending and savings trends than headline GDP figures.
Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics shows household discretionary spending increased by 1.4% in the three months to June 2026, but nearly half of that was from people buying vehicles, particularly electric cars.
Demand for "luxury" services like domestic and international travel was particularly weak, and the "rising cost of living pressures aligned with restrained spending", the ABS said.
That suggests many households are still prioritising essentials and major purchases over discretionary spending.
Similarly, household savings rates have remained relatively high compared to the late 2010s, which can indicate households are being cautious about the future and keeping more money aside where possible.
That's a very different picture to positive GDP growth.
What are economists, investors and policymakers watching most closely?
Experts are watching the inflation rate, the RBA's cash rate decision and further disruptions to oil and gas supply in the Middle East.
If the inflation rate continues to stay stubbornly high or increase further, that would cause general prices to rise again in Australia. The RBA may need to increase the cash rate again in November, increasing the cost of bank loans and leading people to cut back on spending.
Further disruptions to oil and gas supply routes in the Middle East are also a major concern for inflation growth. If oil delays or stoppages continue, that will increase the cost of petrol and push up inflation.
For Slade, the key issue is whether today's cost-of-living concerns start affecting people's confidence in their employment and financial future.
"At the moment people are worried about the cost of living rather than their jobs. If job security concerns start to climb, that's when households really pull back, and that becomes self-fulfilling," he says.
