articles.title: Global Potato Summit 2026 to Highlight Rising Potato Exports and Processing Opportunities in India - PotatoPro
articles.summary: Global Potato Summit 2026 to Highlight Rising Potato Exports and Processing Opportunities in India  PotatoPro
articles.full_text:
Global Potato Summit 2026 will bring together industry leaders to discuss potato processing, export growth and international collaboration. (Image: Global Potato Summit 2025)
Global Potato Summit 2026 to Highlight Rising Potato Exports and Processing Opportunities in India
India’s potato industry is entering a new phase of growth, driven by rising production, expanding food-processing capabilities and rapidly increasing exports of fresh and value-added potato products. With international demand for frozen French fries, dehydrated potato ingredients and processed snacks creating new commercial opportunities, India is strengthening its position as a significant supplier to global markets. At the same time, weather-related production pressures in parts of Europe could create opportunities for Indian growers, processors and exporters to expand their international presence.
Against this backdrop, the second edition of the Global Potato Summit 2026, organised by Media Today Group on December 16–17 in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, will provide a platform to connect the Indian potato industry with international markets, technologies and business opportunities.
Rising Production and Expanding Export Potential
India’s potato production is projected to reach 59.89 million tonnes in 2025–26, compared with 58.57 million tonnes in 2024–25, according to the production estimates cited for the period. This expanding production base supports both domestic consumption and the growing demand for potatoes used in processing, including French fries, chips, flakes, granules and other value-added products.
India’s export performance reflects the changing structure of the industry. According to UN Comtrade data, exports of frozen and prepared potatoes reached approximately USD 279 million in calendar year 2025, compared with USD 203 million in 2024. This represents growth of around 37.5 percent in export value. Export volumes in this broad customs category also increased substantially, reflecting the expanding role of Indian processors in international trade.
Fresh potatoes remain another important component of the export basket, generating approximately USD 88.3 million in 2025. Meanwhile, exports of potato flakes, granules and pellets reached USD 67.8 million, underlining the growing importance of dehydrated potato ingredients in the food-processing industry.
Other categories contributed to the diversification of India’s potato trade. Exports of preserved potatoes were valued at approximately USD 6.9 million, frozen potatoes under a separate customs classification at USD 4.6 million, and potato starch at USD 3 million. Together, these six specified product categories accounted for approximately USD 449.6 million in exports during 2025.  These figures demonstrate that India’s potato export opportunity extends well beyond fresh produce. The industry is increasingly participating in international markets through frozen products, dehydrated ingredients and other processed forms that offer opportunities for greater value addition.
Frozen French Fries Lead the Growth Story
Frozen French fries have emerged as a key driver of India’s potato export growth, supported by investments in processing, improved raw-material availability and rising demand across international food-service markets. Exports of potato flakes and dehydrated ingredients are further expanding opportunities in industrial food manufacturing.
Sustaining this momentum will depend on strengthening the farm-to-factory link through processing-grade varieties, quality seeds, scientific storage and reliable procurement. Closer coordination among growers, processors and exporters will be critical to ensuring consistent quality, improving efficiency and enhancing India’s competitiveness in global markets.
European Supply Pressures Create New Opportunities
Adverse weather conditions are putting pressure on Europe’s potato supplies, potentially opening new opportunities for alternative suppliers. According to the North-Western European Potato Growers (NEPG) forecast, the 2026 ware potato crop across Belgium, France, Germany and the Netherlands could fall to 20.7 million tonnes, down 25.4 percent from 27.75 million tonnes in 2025.
Global Potato Summit 2026 will highlight opportunities for potato processing, value-added products and international trade. (Image: Global Potato Summit 2025)
For India, this presents a potential export opportunity, particularly in processed potato products. However, capitalising on it will require consistent quality, competitive pricing, reliable logistics and compliance with international standards. Diversifying into Asian, Middle Eastern and other markets can further strengthen India’s potato export prospects.
Global Potato Summit 2025: A Catalyst for Multiplier Growth
Recognising the need for a connected and competitive potato value chain, Media Today Group organised the inaugural Global Potato Summit 2025 at India Expo Centre & Mart (IEML), Greater Noida, with support from APEDA and participation from industry and trade organisations.
By bringing growers, processors, exporters, technology providers and machinery manufacturers onto a common platform, the summit connected the dots between farm productivity, post-harvest infrastructure, processing, value addition and export growth. It highlighted how progress in one segment can create opportunities across the entire ecosystem—from better returns for growers and new investments in processing to stronger market linkages and wider access to global markets.
The summit’s larger significance lay in placing these interconnected priorities within a shared growth agenda, reinforcing the potential of collaboration, technology and trade to multiply value across India’s potato economy.
Global Potato Summit 2026: Expanding the International Outlook
Building on the foundation laid in 2025, Media Today Group will organise the second Global Potato Summit on December 16–17, 2026, in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, featuring an international conference on "Transforming India’s Potato Value-Chain for Global Competitiveness."  The summit will address key priorities across the value chain, including seed development, mechanisation, storage, cold-chain infrastructure, processing, packaging and exports, with a focus on technology, innovation and international market access. By connecting growers, processors, equipment manufacturers, packaging companies and exporters, it aims to foster technology partnerships, strengthen industry linkages and accelerate value addition and export growth across India’s potato sector.
From Production Strength to Global Competitiveness
India’s growing potato production and expanding exports provide a strong foundation for further industry development. The next stage will depend on the ability to translate this scale into consistent quality, efficient processing, dependable logistics and sustained access to international markets.
The combined export value of the six specified potato-product categories—approximately USD 449.6 million in 2025—illustrates the diversity of India’s existing trade. Further opportunities could emerge through stronger processing capabilities, product diversification, improved storage infrastructure and deeper engagement with overseas buyers. Through the Global Potato Summit 2026, Media Today Group aims to bring these priorities into focus and encourage closer collaboration across the Indian and international potato industries.
Global Potato Summit 2026 aims to strengthen collaboration among potato growers, processors, exporters and industry organisations. (Image: Global Potato Summit 2025)
As global markets respond to changing production conditions, evolving consumer demand and growing requirements for processed foods, the summit will offer a platform for the industry to explore how India can strengthen its role as a competitive supplier of fresh potatoes and value-added potato products.
Global Potato Summit 2026
The Global Potato Summit 2026 will take place on December 16–17 in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, India, under the theme "Transforming India’s Potato Value-Chain for Global Competitiveness."

articles.title: How the Iran war is ruining Saudi Arabia’s plans - Vox
articles.summary: How the Iran war is ruining Saudi Arabia’s plans  VoxEverything is going wrong for Muhammad bin Salman  The EconomistSaudi Arabia’s Military Limitations Are Being Exposed by Houthi Attacks  WSJWhy the Houthis Are So Hard to Defeat  Bloomberg.comHow Saudi Arabia Created the Yemen It Fears  The National Interest
articles.full_text:
As the US-Iran war drags on, the damage is being felt regionally: Saudi Arabia experienced the worst attack in over a decade earlier this month, when Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi militia struck an airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh. The strike killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 others.
Saudi Arabia responded with missile attacks on Yemen, striking oil facilities, and the Houthis have launched more strikes of their own, targeting Saudi oil infrastructure.
The dueling strikes are the latest development in a decade-plus of conflict between Saudi and the Houthis, a political and military group that controls part of northern Yemen, which had been on pause until earlier this year after a 2022 ceasefire. But the Iran war, and Houthi affiliation with Iran’s network of proxy groups, mean the current violence has far-reaching implications for the US, Israel, and the global energy economy.
It also threatens more than just Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil industry: As Gregg Carlstrom, a Middle East correspondent for The Economist, explains, the attacks cut at the heart of the country’s project to evolve into a destination for foreign investment, travel, tourism, and more. On Monday, the country’s upcoming Future Investment Initiative was postponed until 2027.
Carlstrom, who is based in Riyadh, spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram how the attack has been received inside Saudi Arabia, why it comes at an especially bad time for the country, and how President Donald Trump might — or might not — get more involved.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Can you help us understand how the Houthis have such a presence in the country right now? Are they infiltrating the country? Are they already there?
They’re shooting from outside the country. They’re shooting from Yemen. The Houthis are a group that’s been around for a few decades. They were originally a local insurgency in Yemen that was fighting against the Yemeni government. They originate from the northern part of Yemen, but they were able to gain control of large parts of that country from 2014 onwards. Ali Abdullah Saleh, the longtime dictator of Yemen, was overthrown during the Arab Spring and the Houthis were able to seize a large chunk of territory.
They are effectively in control of most of the population centers in Yemen. They have received increasing support from Iran, which has provided them with weapons, with money, with know-how, and technical expertise. And they have used that to build an arsenal of drones and missiles, which they are using now to carry out attacks on Saudi Arabia.
And was there a particular reason they targeted the airport in Riyadh? Were they trying to send a message here?
If you listen to the messaging from the Houthis, they are trying to describe this as almost a like-for-like campaign, where you’ve had years in which the Saudi-led coalition, which invaded Yemen in 2015, has been imposing a blockade of Yemeni airspace, has been restricting flights in and out of that country.
And so the Houthis describe this publicly as being a retaliation in kind, but I think they’ve also just figured out that attacks on airports are a very effective way to cause economic disruption in Saudi Arabia. You prevent not just people from flying in and out but also, as we’ve seen disruptions to shipping via the Strait of Hormuz, a lot of cargo that these countries depend on for daily needs are coming in by air instead.
Carrying out these sorts of attacks, shutting down the airport in a capital city, is a very effective way for the Houthis to impose economic pain on the Saudis.
And I guess on some level it makes the country feel insecure. How is that making Saudi Arabia’s leader feel right now? What’s his response been?
It comes at a very difficult time for the Saudi leadership because they are supposed to be hosting a number of events this month where Saudi will be playing a role on the world stage.
There’s something called the World Petroleum Congress that is taking place this week [October 11–15], which is normally a big event that draws executives from top oil and gas companies. Many of them canceled their participation because of the attacks on the airport.
Then they are supposed to be hosting the [now-postponed] Future Investment Initiative, which is something often known outside Saudi Arabia as “Davos in the Desert.” It’s the sort of flagship investment conference that takes place here every year. It draws a who’s who of global finance.
For a country that is trying to diversify its economy, a country that is trying to attract foreign investment and make itself into a hub for finance and travel and tourism, these sorts of attacks are very detrimental to those goals.
And this is coming as Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the rest of the leadership in the country is really trying to establish Saudi Arabia as the premier economic hub in the region. The stakes are really high for him right now?
They are. And just about everything that they are trying to do is being disrupted by what’s happened over the past few weeks.
If you look at travel, for example, the Public Investment Fund, which is the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, last year launched a new airline, Riyadh Air, which they are hoping will eventually compete with Emirates or Qatar Airways, the really big carriers in the Gulf.
That airline was just getting into regular operations this summer where they were growing their fleet, they were growing their network of destinations. And then suddenly this happens and their home base in Riyadh is shut down. They have moved some of their planes out of Riyadh to other airports to keep them safe from Houthi attacks. Obviously, it’s very disruptive for trying to build an air carrier.
In Riyadh itself, the financial district — this sort of long-planned attempt to set up a banking hub that might rival the one in Dubai — had just started to get going over the past couple of years, when you had banks and other financial services firms moving in there. Everybody who works there has now been told to work remotely for the foreseeable future because there is a concern about possible Houthi attacks against skyscrapers and the financial district.
Everything they are trying to do, from finance to travel to trade, all of it is being disrupted and threatened by what’s happening in Yemen.
What options does he have to reassure investors and the world really that he can protect the country and maybe especially his airport, where a bunch of the investment is focused?
The airport, I think, is going to be difficult to reassure people about. You can install additional air defenses there. You can move more batteries and more interceptors there, but at the end of the day, no air defense system is hermetic. There’s no 100 percent guarantee that you’re going to shoot down every incoming projectile.
As long as there is this ongoing war between the Houthis and Yemen and the Saudis, I think people might have ongoing concerns about the airport. You have to resolve that underlying issue to give people confidence.
Now, how do you try to resolve that? If you’re Saudi Arabia right now, you have two bad options. One is you keep fighting. You try to militarily defeat the Houthis or at least force them to accept a renewed ceasefire.
The other option is you cut a deal. You try to offer the Houthis some concessions that might encourage them to go back to the ceasefire. That’s going to be very costly for Saudi Arabia. I’ve heard that the Houthis are demanding probably billions of dollars of financial concessions where they would want the Saudis to offer some money for reconstruction and to pay the salaries of Yemeni civil servants working in Houthi-controlled areas.
If you are the Saudi leadership right now, neither one is really a good option.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has a pretty strong relationship with the president of the United States, who’s very sympathetic to Saudi Arabia and Saudi investment. Has he appealed to President Trump for help here yet?
He has. He’s done so repeatedly over the past month or so, asking not just for support with the Saudi campaign in Yemen, but for America to carry out its own airstrikes in Yemen. And the response so far from Donald Trump has been to refuse that.
For the US to get involved in a bigger way, there are some practical constraints at the moment where a lot of American military assets are tied up in the Strait of Hormuz trying to keep that open, keep oil flowing through the Strait. And so the response from Trump has been disappointing for the Saudi Crown prince. The US is providing intelligence support. It’s helping on that front, but it is not directly getting involved in the war in Yemen.

articles.title: ASEAN-Russia Trade and Investment: October 2026 Updates - russia's pivot to asia
articles.summary: ASEAN-Russia Trade and Investment: October 2026 Updates  russia's pivot to asia
articles.full_text:
ASEAN-Russia bilateral trade reached about US$18 billion in 2025, while investment from ASEAN member states into the Russian economy stood at US$3.2 billion and Russian investment in Southeast Asia totalled US$7.1 billion. Bilateral trade has increased by 10% in H1 2026, meaning the commercial agenda is now widening beyond traditional energy and commodity exchanges to include agricultural supplies, food security, fertilisers, digital services, logistics, manufacturing, technology and investment partnerships. The next stage will depend on whether businesses can turn these established trade flows into new supply contracts, distribution networks and long-term investment projects. This article explains these development dynamics and is essential reading for anyone involved in Russian and ASEAN affairs.
The immediate Russian trade and investment opportunities are visible across Southeast Asia. Vietnam recorded US$4.77 billion in bilateral trade with Russia in 2025, while Indonesia’s trade approached US$5 billion. Thailand’s trade reached approximately US$1.7 billion, and Cambodia’s exports to Russia rose from US$2.9 million in 2025 to US$15.6 million in the first eight months of 2026. Russian agricultural exports to ASEAN totalled US$251 million in January-May 2026, an increase of 5% year on year, with Thailand and Vietnam accounting for more than 70% of the total. These figures point to an uneven but expanding commercial relationship, with established markets providing scale and smaller economies offering opportunities for new products and suppliers.
ASEAN’s Moscow Visit Connects Business Priorities with the 2035 Trade Programme
Against this commercial backdrop, ASEAN Secretary-General Dr Kao Kim Hourn visited Moscow from October 12 to 15, 2026, for discussions on expanding economic cooperation. His meetings on October 13 included Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Deputy Minister of Digital Development, Communications and Mass Media Bella Cherkesova, Presidential Adviser Anton Kobyakov, and Russia-ASEAN Business Council Chairman Ivan Polyakov. On October 14, he met Russian Minister of Science and Higher Education Valery Falkov and members of the ASEAN Committee in Moscow. His programme also included engagement with the Eurasian Economic Commission and participation in Russian Energy Week and an international conference at MGIMO University.
These discussions were particularly relevant to companies seeking commercial partners. Kao and Polyakov, together with representatives of the Russian business community, examined opportunities in energy, food security, agriculture, supply-chain connectivity and digital transformation. They also discussed more regular business missions, business-matching activities and investment partnerships intended to generate practical commercial outcomes. The available announcements do not provide a participant count, a list of all participating companies, or the value of contracts signed at this meeting. It is therefore more accurate to treat the engagement as business development and partnership-building rather than as a completed investment transaction.
Kao’s visit followed the 15th ASEAN Economic Ministers-Russia Consultation, held in Manila on September 22, 2026, at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City. Philippine Department of Trade and Industry Secretary Ma. Cristina A. Roque and Russian Deputy Minister of Economic Development Vladimir Ilyichev co-chaired the meeting, which Kao also attended. The ministers endorsed the ASEAN-Russia Strategic Programme on Trade and Investment Cooperation for 2026-2035. Its 11 areas are trade and investment, digital transformation, science and technology, transport, agriculture, energy, mining, climate change, the circular economy, tourism and the creative economy. The programme gives the commercial relationship a longer-term structure, but its significance will be measured through implementation. Businesses need workable customs procedures, reliable payments, clear technical requirements, transport links and commercially viable contracts. The parallel ASEAN-Eurasian Economic Commission programme for 2026-2030 offers a technical channel for addressing these issues. A joint seminar on customs regulation and Single Window mechanisms took place by videoconference on January 28, 2026, with further technical seminars on energy, e-commerce, agriculture and technical regulation planned for late 2026. EAEU-ASEAN Days are planned for Moscow in the first quarter of 2027.
Vietnam: The Clearest Demonstration of Public and Company-Level Trade Expansion
Vietnam is among the strongest examples of how regional cooperation can connect with direct business activity. Bilateral trade reached US$4.77 billion in 2025, up 4% year on year. Vietnamese exports to Russia were nearly US$2.26 billion, while imports from Russia totalled US$2.51 billion. During January-July 2026, trade reached US$3.24 billion, an increase of 12%, comprising US$1.33 billion in Vietnamese exports and US$1.91 billion in imports from Russia. Full-year trade is expected to exceed US$5 billion if the momentum continues.
On September 21, more than 100 Vietnamese companies and 29 Russian companies participated in a business-to-business networking programme in Ho Chi Minh City. The discussions covered agriculture, food, chemicals, fertilisers, mechanical engineering, manufacturing, information technology and logistics. Thirty Vietnamese companies had also showcased agricultural and food products at WorldFood Moscow 2026, seeking to expand their Russian-market presence. The product mix offers scope for two-way expansion. Vietnam supplies textiles and garments, coffee, seafood, electronics and consumer goods, while Russian exports include coal, fertilisers, chemicals, plastics, metals and meat.
The Vietnam-EAEU Free Trade Agreement provides an existing route for tariff reductions and market access. The next commercial opportunity lies in moving from individual shipments towards processing, contract manufacturing, technology transfer, local distribution and longer-term purchasing arrangements.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has introduced a visa-free regime for Vietnamese citizens for one year, taking effect from October 15, 2026. On 15 October 2026, Russia and Vietnam held the 37th meeting of the Intergovernmental Coordinating Committee of the Joint Tropical Research and Technology Centre in Moscow, approving a joint scientific research programme for 2027 covering infectious diseases, marine science and specialist training. In June 2026, researchers conducted their first full-scale joint marine expedition aboard the Professor Gagarinsky, and in September 2026, they opened a Russian-equipped infectious disease research laboratory; more than 400 Russian researchers and specialists participated in the centre’s activities during 2026.
Both countries agreed to continue joint research, organise another marine expedition in 2027, expand internships for Vietnamese specialists at Russian universities and research institutes, and prepare for the centre’s 40th anniversary in 2028. On 14-17 October 2026, the 2nd Russia-Vietnam People’s Diplomacy Forum took place in Saint Petersburg, with nearly 150 delegates attending to strengthen the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership through economic, cultural, educational, scientific and local-level cooperation; on 16 October, a thematic economic session launched a joint report by the Vietnam-Russia Knowledge Network, ANO Coordination Laboratory and Saint Petersburg Committee for External Relations. The report identified opportunities in technology, clean energy, civilian nuclear technology, LNG infrastructure, agriculture, food processing and maritime logistics, while recommending removal of technical trade barriers, harmonisation of standards, investment in warehousing, direct shipping routes and stronger digital-market strategies
Indonesia: Crude Oil, Maritime Links, Satellite and Media Cooperation
On 16 October 2026, Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom signed an agreement with Indonesia’s PT Pembangkit Listrik Nuklir during Russian Energy Week to supply electricity to North Maluku in eastern Indonesia, particularly northern Halmahera Island, using two PEB-100 floating nuclear power units with a combined capacity of 200 MW. Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev described the deal as the world’s first export agreement to supply electricity from a floating nuclear power unit, highlighting government support and private-sector participation in developing large-scale nuclear energy infrastructure.

articles.title: 27 South African food companies seek export opportunities in France - FreshPlaza
articles.summary: 27 South African food companies seek export opportunities in France  FreshPlaza
articles.full_text:
Twenty-seven South African food manufacturing companies will seek export opportunities and commercial partnerships in France when they participate in the SIAL Paris International Food Products Exhibition from 17-21 October 2026. The companies will receive support from the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (the dtic), which will host a South African National Pavilion.
Drawn from six provinces, the companies will showcase locally manufactured products, including processed foods, non-alcoholic beverages, preserved foods, spices, soups, frozen products, health and organic products, confectionery, and gourmet food products.
SIAL Paris brings together manufacturers, distributors, restaurateurs, importers, exporters, and other international food industry participants, providing opportunities to engage potential buyers and explore commercial partnerships.
According to the Acting Deputy Director-General of Exports at the dtic, Mr Willem van der Spuy, South Africa's participation forms part of efforts to increase exports of value-added products, diversify international markets, and support companies in establishing export relationships.
"France is an important market in South Africa's export diversification agenda and a strategic economic partner. Our objective is not simply to showcase South African products, but to use platforms such as SIAL Paris to connect export-ready companies with buyers, importers, distributors and other commercial partners who can assist them to establish and expand their presence in the French and broader European markets," says Van der Spuy.
He adds that the dtic is placing greater emphasis on targeted business-to-business matchmaking to connect participating companies with relevant buyers and ensure follow-up after the exhibition.
"We want to strengthen the commercial outcomes from our international engagements. This means increasing targeted B2B matchmaking, generating quality business leads and supporting companies to convert those opportunities into export orders, distribution partnerships and sustainable market relationships," says Van der Spuy.
The department's support for international exhibition participation is intended to expand South Africa's exporter base, increase exports of value-added manufactured products, and help companies expand their operations as they secure international customers.
"The real measure of success is what happens beyond the exhibition. When a South African company secures a new buyer, enters a new market or expands an existing export relationship, this creates the basis for increased production, business growth and employment. This is the commercial impact that we want our export promotion programme to increasingly deliver," adds Van der Spuy.
South Africa's participation forms part of the dtic's efforts to strengthen commercial relations in international markets through market exposure, targeted buyer engagement, and follow-up aimed at converting export opportunities into commercial agreements.

articles.title: Export tax reduced to 0%: A boost for Vietnamese fertilizers to reach further markets. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Export tax reduced to 0%: A boost for Vietnamese fertilizers to reach further markets.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| The proposal to reduce export taxes to 0% is expected to help fertilizer businesses alleviate oversupply pressure and increase their competitiveness in the international market - Photo: PV | 
 The paradox of "growth but still fraught with difficulties"
 The year 2026 is witnessing significant progress for Vietnam's fertilizer industry on the international trade map. According to data from the Customs Department, in the first nine months of 2026 alone, Vietnam's fertilizer exports reached approximately 2.2 million tons, bringing in nearly 1.2 billion USD in revenue.
 Compared to the same period last year, this figure represents a 31.6% increase in volume and a jump of 69% in value. The growth rate in export value far exceeding that of volume is a positive sign, reflecting an improvement in average export prices or effective shifts in the structure of export goods.
 However, from an economic perspective, these optimistic figures cannot mask a multifaceted picture fraught with concerns. Positive export results do not necessarily mean that all businesses are sailing smoothly in their production and operations. In reality, many domestic manufacturers are facing a paradox: production capacity exceeds domestic consumption, yet they still struggle to compete with imported goods. At the same time, when striving to bring their products to the global market, they encounter cost barriers and disadvantages from current tax policies.
 A prime example of oversupply in the domestic market is urea fertilizer. According to Ms. Nguyen Thi Hien, Deputy General Director of the Ca Mau Petroleum Fertilizer Corporation, the demand for urea in the Vietnamese market currently fluctuates between 1.6 and 1.8 million tons per year. Meanwhile, the total capacity of the four domestic urea production plants has reached approximately 2.6 million tons per year. This imbalance between supply and demand creates a huge potential surplus of 800,000 to 1 million tons annually.
 The pressure intensifies as the domestic market annually has to share market share with approximately 309,000-400,000 tons of urea imported from China, Indonesia , and other sources. With businesses struggling to find outlets for surplus goods while facing intense price competition in their own market, exports have become a vital lifeline to maintain factory operations. However, the 5% export tax in the international market is proving to be a major obstacle.
 Not only urea, but superphosphate fertilizers are also facing the same situation. Current tax policies create a large disparity between products. The fact that superphosphate is subject to a 5% tax while many other items enjoy a 0% tax has reduced the competitiveness of Vietnamese goods against competitors not subject to tax, while also increasing inventory pressure. In addition, NPK fertilizer manufacturers also report difficulties due to import taxes on raw materials (phosphate and potassium fertilizers), followed by export taxes on finished products, significantly increasing costs.
 Policy impetus: Harmonizing the interests of businesses and farmers.
 Recognizing these bottlenecks, the Ministry of Finance has taken strong steps to address them by submitting a draft decree amending and supplementing several articles of Decree No. 26 to the Ministry of Justice for appraisal. Most notably, the proposal includes adjusting the export tax rate for three strategic commodities – urea, superphosphate, and potassium sulfate (SOP) – from 5% down to 0%.
 This is considered a timely policy leverage. Reducing the tax rate to 0% will directly cut financial obligations, creating more room for price competitiveness for businesses in the international market. For example, for an export shipment with a taxable value of 10 billion VND, the new policy will help businesses save 500 million VND immediately. This practical support makes it easier for businesses to bid, sign contracts, and expand their markets.
 Some concerns have been raised that boosting exports could increase domestic fertilizer prices. However, analysts argue that this conclusion cannot be automatically drawn. For urea, domestic production capacity far exceeds demand, providing a solid buffer to ensure stable supply. Furthermore, domestic fertilizer prices are influenced by a range of macroeconomic variables such as import volumes, seasonal demand, and global input prices (gas, energy). If supply remains stable and input prices cool down, fertilizer prices can certainly remain at a favorable level. However, policy management still needs to be considered from a dual perspective: simultaneously creating a springboard for exports while ensuring farmers have access to goods at reasonable retail prices at the right time for the planting season.
 As we enter the final months of 2026, the fertilizer export market is opening up many growth opportunities if international demand remains positive. The proposed reduction of tariffs to 0% will be a breath of fresh air, helping major manufacturers clear inventory and improve efficiency. However, to succeed in the harsh international market, businesses, especially those dependent on imported raw materials, still need a proactive and astute strategy for managing costs, transportation, and exchange rates.

articles.title: Latest jobs dataset confirms Australia leads the world again - Independent Australia
articles.summary: Latest jobs dataset confirms Australia leads the world again  Independent Australia
articles.full_text:
While the Albanese Government guides the economy ever higher in global rankings, the malignant newsrooms escalate their destructive falsehoods, as Alan Austin reports.
Six years ago, as the world battled the COVID pandemic, Australia’s economy was a conspicuous loser among the 38 wealthy members of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
The jobless rate of 6.92% ranked a dismal 18th. Economic growth in the first two quarters of 2020 was negative 0.16% and negative 6.79%, confirming Australia was in its deepest recession since the 1930s. Government debt blew out from 10.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) to 28.3%, escalating interest payments for decades to come.
Interest rates collapsed through 2020 to the all-time low of 0.1%, condemning thousands of elderly retirees to poverty and homelessness.
Fast forward to September 2026 and we find Australia’s jobless rate has tumbled to 4.72%, which now ranks a creditable tenth in the OECD.
Australia is one of only two economies in the world with triple A credit ratings, with both the jobless rate and inflation below 5% and government debt below 19% of GDP. The other is Switzerland.
Australia is the only triple-A economy with interest rates in the optimum band of 3.75% to 5% and wealth per adult above $865,000.
Yet the media companies which happily supported the re-election of the disastrous former Coalition are now mercilessly attacking Labor.
Mixed news on jobs
An impartial assessment of the September employment numbers, issued by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) last Thursday, notes many positives and some negatives.
The seasonally adjusted jobless rate has edged up slightly to 4.72%, as in the rest of the world, since U.S. President Donald Trump’s senseless tariffs and destructive invasions have disrupted global commerce.
The Reserve Bank (RBA) has argued, however, that a temporary lift in unemployment will benefit everyone in the long term.
Other significant outcomes include:
- full-time jobs increased by 34,400 in September; part-time and seasonal jobs decreased by 73,700; total jobs fell by 39,300;
- the jobless rate remaining below 5% has stretched to an impressive 59 months;
- underemployment – employed workers needing more hours – was 6.33%, bringing the streak of months below 6.7% to 58;
- job participation at 66.76% remains within the narrow optimum band 66.4% to 67.2% where it has been for 47 months;
- 69,100 workers have been jobless for more than two years, down from 84,500 when Labor took office; and
- Treasurer Jim Chalmers has added 1.33 million total jobs, a record relative to population only exceeded by Paul Keating.
Solid global comparisons
Where employment numbers – and the Albanese Government’s economic performance overall – are seen to be most impressive are in global rankings.
Since September 2020, Australia’s jobless rate has plummeted from 6.92% to 4.72%, one of the world’s best improvements.
Over that period, unemployment has worsened in New Zealand, Germany, Finland, Iceland, Hungary, Luxembourg and the Czech Republic.
New Zealand, Belgium, Poland and Portugal now have unemployment above 5.5%. It is above 6% in Canada, Germany, Italy, Greece and Austria; above 8% in France and Sweden; and above 9% in Spain, Finland, Chile and Colombia.
Newsrooms destroy social cohesion
Australia’s craven news media are determined never to report the economy accurately. They want to wreck the Albanese Government, even if this undermines consumer confidence, life satisfaction and the nation’s mental health.
The Nine network headed its report on the latest jobs data: ‘Unemployment shock as jobless rate hits five-year high, nearly 40,000 Aussies fall out of work.’
Seven News asked, ‘Has Labor lost control of the economy?’
The Australian led with ‘Self-sabotage warning to ALP amid jobs slump’.
The Murdoch tabloids ran with ‘Jim’s done a job on us: 40,000 fewer people in work as businesses suffer’.
Reporting was just as irresponsible and harmful in the Australian Financial Review, InDaily, The Saturday Paper and The Guardian.
Coverage across the Tasman
New Zealand’s economy is vastly worse than Australia’s on virtually every measurable outcome.
Quarterly GDP growth has been negative in three of the last nine quarters, annual GDP growth negative for four of the last eight quarters, inflation is higher than Australia’s at 4.1% and government debt to GDP is more than double at 41.8%.
Interest rates have been below 3% for more than a year, ensuring many elderly savers who rely on interest payments stay in deep poverty.
Yet New Zealand’s newsrooms report these outcomes neutrally, without malicious accusations and blatant lies.
When the latest jobs data showed worsening unemployment, The New Zealand Herald simply headed its report: ‘Unemployment rate hits 5.6% — worse than expectations.’
It quoted the spokesperson for the statistics bureau – then Finance Minister Nicola Willis – and finally a Westpac senior economist.
The report highlighted all the positives, with no criticism of the administration from the Opposition or anyone else.
Coverage by Radio New Zealand (RNZ) was similarly calm and factual, emphasising the forces against the Government, and protecting national morale and social cohesion.
RNZ headed its broadcast, ‘New unemployment figures hit 11-year high’.
It accepted at face value the obvious explanation for the setbacks — that Trump’s manifest follies are impacting all trading partners.
RNZ's economics correspondent Gyles Beckford found no fault whatsoever with the national Government:
“That’s just the state of the economy. Now we might also say it might be the volatility and uncertainty that’s been caused by the U.S.-Iran war. It could be the rise in fuel costs making businesses cautious... All these things go into the mix and at the moment, it is just a weak labour market.”
That would never be broadcast by Australia’s malevolent newsrooms. Everything that happens is bad. And everything bad is Labor’s fault. Albo must be sacked!
Such is Australia’s doom.
Alan Austin is an Independent Australia columnist and freelance journalist. You can follow him on Twitter @alanaustin001 and Bluesky @alanaustin.bsky.social.

articles.title: Malaysia’s exports hit five-year high in September as electronics shipments jump - The Edge Malaysia
articles.summary: Malaysia’s exports hit five-year high in September as electronics shipments jump  The Edge Malaysia
articles.full_text:
Imports, meanwhile, climbed 52.7% to RM181.4 billion in September, also exceeding the Bloomberg survey’s forecast of 39% growth. (Photo by Zahid Izzani/The Edge)
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 19): Malaysian exports rose to its highest in five years in September as electronics shipments expanded sharply while orders from key markets like the US and China soared.
Exports totalled RM215.1 billion, an increase of 54.5% year-on-year, according to data released by the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (Miti) on Monday. The expansion exceeded the median forecast of 39.9% in a Bloomberg survey and accelerated from August’s 45.5% growth.
“Malaysia’s trade performance remains exposed to uncertainties arising from shifting trade policies by major economies and geopolitical tensions,” the ministry said.
The ongoing conflicts in West Asia, in particular, could disrupt global trade flows and intensify cost pressures, Miti said, adding that it will continue to “assess these developments, strengthen market diversification, expand access to high-growth markets and help Malaysian exporters adapt”.
Electrical and electronics, which accounted for more than half of the total exports, jumped 68% and reported a new monthly record high. Optical and scientific equipment, such as specialised medical gear and semiconductor test instruments, also reported their highest monthly export value.
Exports of petroleum products climbed 33% while liquefied natural gas surged 46%.
By destination, exports to the US recorded a 72% gain while deliveries to China, the biggest trading partner of Malaysia, were 52% higher. Shipments to Taiwan and South Korea both more than doubled.
By end use, imports of intermediate goods — semi-finished goods used in final assembly of products such as computers or cars — climbed 69.6% to RM92.1 billion. Capital goods imports increased 20.9% while consumption goods rose 18.2%.
All in all, Malaysia reported a trade surplus of RM33.7 billion in September, widening 65% year-on-year and 20% month-on-month.

Proposed Project:
The U.S. National Science Foundation Regional Innovation Engines (Engines) program, led by NSF's Directorate for Technology, Innovation and Partnerships (TIP), is NSF's flagship investment in place-based innovation. Established pursuant to the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022, the program invests in regions across the United States to bring together the research, talent, partnerships, and resources needed to turn advances in science and technology into economic and societal benefits. Each NSF Engine serves a defined geographic Region of Service (RoS), the area intended to benefit from the NSF Engine's activities and investments, and is organized around technologies and challenges important to that region and the Nation.
Specifically, the program seeks to:
Advance key technology areas critical to U.S. competitiveness;
Address pressing national and societal challenges;
Cultivate partnerships across industry, academia, government, nonprofit organizations, civil society and communities of practice;
Promote economic growth and job creation; and
Develop the regional workforce and talent needed to sustain innovation.
Each NSF Engine carries out these objectives through three core functions: use-inspired research and development, translation of innovation results to society, and workforce development. Together, these activities are intended to strengthen a RoS's capacity to develop and commercialize new technologies, create and grow businesses, prepare workers for new opportunities, and attract additional investment. Over time, NSF Engines are expected to develop into sustainable regional innovation ecosystems that contribute to economic growth and U.S. competitiveness.
NSF Engines are substantial, long-term investments. Each NSF Engine may receive NSF funding for up to 10 years, based on its performance and progress toward established goals and milestones. As NSF Engines develop, their activities, partnerships, and sources of support are expected to grow and evolve. Regular reporting on a defined cadence helps NSF Engines teams track performance, identify and address issues, and adjust their strategies as needed. At the same time, it allows NSF to assess progress across the portfolio, identify risks and emerging challenges, and make informed program management and funding decisions.

AGENCY:
Veterans Health Administration, Department of Veterans Affairs.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
Veterans Health Administration (VHA), Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), is announcing an opportunity for public comment on the proposed collection of certain information by the agency. Under the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) of 1995, Federal agencies are required to publish a notice in the
Federal Register
concerning each proposed collection of information, including each proposed extension of a currently approved collection, and allow 60 days for public comment in response to the notice. DATES: Comments must be received on or before December 21, 2026.
VA PRA information:
Dorothy Glasgow, 202-461-1084,
VAPRA@va.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Under the PRA of 1995, Federal agencies must obtain approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for each collection of information they conduct or sponsor. This request for comment is being made pursuant to Section 3506(c)(2)(A) of the PRA.
With respect to the following collection of information, VHA invites comments on: (1) whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of VHA's functions, including whether the information will have practical utility; (2) the accuracy of VHA's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information; (3) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (4) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on respondents, including through the use of automated collection techniques or the use of other forms of information technology.
Title:
State Veterans Homes Construction & Acquisition Grant Program (SVHCGP), VA Forms 10-0388-1, 10-0388-2, 10-0388-3, 10-0388-4, 10-0388-5, 10-0388-6, 10-0388-7, 10-0388-8, 10-0388-9, 10-0388-10, 10-0388-12, 10-0388-13.
OMB Control Number: 2900-0661. https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRASearch
(Once at this link, you can enter the OMB Control Number to find the historical versions of this Information Collection).
Type of Review:
Revision of a currently approved collection.
Abstract:
This collection of information is authorized under 38 U.S.C. 8133(a) and 8135(a), which appropriate the expenditure of funds for State Home Domiciliary, Nursing Home, and Hospital Care. These sections of the U.S.C. require, among other things, that the State government or recognized Federal tribe (government) applicant provide the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) with an application package. Only State governments and Federally recognized tribes (their governments) may submit the information to complete an application for the State Veterans Homes Construction & Acquisition Grant Program (SVHCGP); private groups or citizens are not eligible.
Applicants will complete VA Forms 10-0388-1, 10-0388-2, 10-0388-3, 10-
( printed page 66406)
0388-4, 10-0388-5, 10-0388-6, 10-0388-7, 10-0388-8, 10-0388-9, 10-0388-10, 10-0388-12, and 10-0388-13 to apply for the SVHCGP and certify compliance with VA requirements. VA will use this information, along with other documents submitted by the State and Federally recognized tribe applicants, to evaluate the feasibility of the projects for VA participation and determine eligibility for grant awards. There is a decrease in the estimated number of annual responses and burden hours based upon program data since the last PRA clearance and the projected number of annual applicants.
Affected Public:
State, Local, or Tribal Governments.
Estimated Annual Burden:
720 hours.
Estimated Average Burden per Respondent:
24 hours.

                    SUMMARY:
In compliance with the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) of 1995, this notice announces that the Veterans Benefits Administration, Department of Veterans Affairs, will submit the collection of information abstracted below to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and comment. The PRA submission describes the nature of the information collection and its expected cost and burden and it includes the actual data collection instrument.
                    DATES:
Comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection should be sent by November 19, 2026.
                    ADDRESSES:
                        To submit comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection, please type the following link into your browser: 
                        www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain,
                         select “Currently under Review—Open for Public Comments”, then search the list for the information collection by Title or “OMB Control No. 2900-0110.”
                    
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
                    Title:
                     Application for Assumption Approval and/or Release from Personal Liability to the Government on a Home Loan.
                
                    OMB Control Number:
                     2900-0110 
                    https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRASearch.
                    Type of Review:
                     Revision of a Currently Approved Collection.
                
                    Abstract:
                     VA Form 26-6381, Application for Assumption Approval and/or Release from Personal Liability to the Government on a Home Loan is completed by Veterans who are selling their homes by assumption rather than requiring purchasers to obtain their own financing to pay off the loan. The data furnished on the form is essential to determinations for assumption approval, release of liability, and substitution of entitlement in accordance with 38 U.S.C. 3713(a) and 3714 and 3702(b)(2). AGENCY:
Federal Railroad Administration (FRA), Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
This document provides the public notice that the Maryland Department of Transportation Maryland Transit Administration MARC Train Service (MACZ), petitioned FRA to extend a special approval of an alternate standard for periodic brake equipment maintenance.
DATES:
FRA must receive comments on the petition by December 21, 2026. FRA will consider comments received after that date to the extent practicable.
ADDRESSES:
Comments:
Comments related to this docket may be submitted by going to
https://www.regulations.gov
and following the online instructions for submitting comments.
Instructions:
All submissions must include the agency name and docket number. All comments received will be posted without change to
https://www.regulations.gov;
this includes any personal information. Please see the Privacy Act heading in the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section of this document for Privacy Act information related to any submitted comments or materials.
Docket:
For access to the docket to read background documents or comments received, go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and follow the online instructions for accessing the docket.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Steven Zuiderveen, Railroad Safety Specialist, FRA Motive Power & Equipment Division, telephone: 202-493-6337, email:
steven.zuiderveen@dot.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Under part 211 of title 49 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), this document provides the public notice that by letter dated April 27, 2026, MACZ petitioned FRA for an extension of a special approval of an alternate standard for periodic brake equipment maintenance per 49 CFR parts 229 (Railroad Locomotive Safety Standards) and 238 (Passenger Equipment Safety Standards). The relevant Docket Number is FRA-2008-0065.
Specifically, MACZ requests approval to continue applying alternate standards for the CCB-KE-3.9 air brake system of the MARC HHP-8 locomotive fleet. This alternate standard to 49 CFR 229.29(e),
Air brake system calibration, maintenance, and testing,
and 238.309(a)(2),
Periodic brake equipment maintenance—General,
allows for an increase in the level two and level three maintenance intervals to 2,944 days (8 years). MACZ explains that it continues
( printed page 66388)
to maintain the air brake systems in accordance with the existing conditions of relief in this docket, and that it has realized a high level of reliability with the air brake system. Further, MACZ indicates that the locomotives are expected to continue in passenger service for MACZ, operated and maintained by Amtrak on the Northeast Corridor, for the foreseeable future.
A copy of the petition, as well as any written communications concerning the petition, is available for review online at
www.regulations.gov.
Interested parties are invited to participate in these proceedings by submitting written views, data, or comments. FRA does not anticipate scheduling a public hearing in connection with these proceedings since the facts do not appear to warrant a hearing. If any interested party desires an opportunity for oral comment and a public hearing, they should notify FRA, in writing, before the end of the comment period and specify the basis for their request.
Communications received by December 21, 2026 will be considered by FRA before final action is taken. Comments received after that date will be considered if practicable.
Privacy Act
Anyone can search the electronic form of any written communications and comments received into any of FRA's dockets by the name of the individual submitting the comment (or signing the document, if submitted on behalf of an association, business, labor union, etc.). Under 5 U.S.C. 553(c), DOT solicits comments from the public to inform its processes. DOT posts these comments, without edit, including any personal information the commenter provides, to
www.regulations.gov,
as described in the system of records notice (DOT/ALL-14 FDMS), which can be reviewed at
https://www.transportation.gov/privacy.
See also
https://www.regulations.gov/privacy-notice
for the privacy notice of
regulations.gov.
Issued in Washington, DC.
John Karl Alexy,
Associate Administrator for Railroad Safety, Chief Safety Officer.

Title:

OMB Control Number:
2900-0936.
https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRASearch.
(Once at this link, you can enter the OMB Control Number to find the historical versions of this Information Collection).
Type of Review:

Abstract:
Section 403 of the John S.
McCain III, Daniel K.
Akaka, and Samuel R.
Johnson VA Maintaining Internal Systems and Strengthening Integrated Outside Networks (MISSION) Act of 2018 (Public Law 115-182; as codified at 38 U.
S.
C.
7302) mandated that VA create a pilot program to establish additional graduate medical education (GME) physician residency placement positions at certain covered facilities.
The pilot program has been implemented and places no fewer than 100 resident physicians at covered facilities (sites) operated by Indian tribe or tribal organization (25 U.
S.
C.
5304), Indian Health Service, Federally-Qualified Health Centers (42 U.
S.
C.
1396d(1)(2)(B)) and Department of Defense.
Participants in this program are required by the statute to collect and provide VA with programmatic data.
VA is required to include this information in an annual Congressionally Mandated Report until the program terminates on August 7, 2031.
The information will continue to be collected by the GME sponsoring institutions and the physician residents they place in the participating covered facilities.
The sponsors themselves will determine the best method for collecting the necessary data, depending on their own resources and staffing.
The information collected includes required elements, such as number of patients seen per day by each resident placed in a covered facility, and consolidated data from the GME sponsoring institutions.
VA will submit this information in an annual report to Congress on continued implementation of the pilot program.

110.

1,800 hours.

AGENCY:
Bureau of Indian Affairs, Interior.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This rule provides for annual adjustments to the level of civil monetary penalties contained in Bureau of Indian Affairs (Bureau) regulations to account for inflation under the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act Improvements Act of 2015 and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) guidance.
DATES:
This rule is effective on October 20, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
This rule may be found on the internet at
https://www.regulations.gov
by entering “RIN 1076-AF81” in the search box.
Alternative Format:

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
, individuals can obtain this document in an alternate format, usable by people with disabilities, at the Office of the Assistant Secretary—Indian Affairs, Room 4660, 1849 C Street NW, Washington, DC 20240.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Oliver Whaley, Director, Office of Regulatory Affairs and Collaborative Action (RACA), Office of the Assistant Secretary—Indian Affairs; Department of the Interior,
RACA@bia.gov;
telephone (202) 738-6065. Individuals in the United States who are deaf, deafblind, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability may dial 711 (TTY, TDD, or TeleBraille) to access telecommunications relay services.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
II. Calculation of 2026 Annual Adjustments
III. Procedural Requirements
A. Regulatory Planning and Review (Executive Order (E.O.s) 12866 and 14192)
B. Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. 601et seq.)
C. Congressional Review Act (CRA)
D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (2 U.S.C. 1501et seq.)
On November 2, 2015, the President signed into law the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act Improvements Act of 2015 (sec. 701 of Pub. L. 114-74) (“the Act”). The Act requires Federal agencies to adjust the level of civil monetary penalties with an initial “catch-up” adjustment through rulemaking and then make subsequent annual adjustments for inflation. The purpose of these adjustments is to
( printed page 66287)
maintain the deterrent effect of civil penalties and to further the policy goals of the underlying statutes.
The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) issued guidance for Federal agencies on calculating the catch-up adjustment.
See
February 24, 2016, Memorandum for the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies, from Shaun Donovan, Director, Office of Management and Budget, re:
Implementation of the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act Improvements Act of 2015
(M-16-06). Under the guidance, the Department identified applicable civil monetary penalties and calculated the catch-up adjustment. A civil monetary penalty is any assessment with a dollar amount that is levied for a violation of a Federal civil statute or regulation, and is assessed or enforceable through a civil action in Federal court or an administrative proceeding. A civil monetary penalty does not include a penalty levied for violation of a criminal statute, or fees for services, licenses, permits, or other regulatory review. The calculated catch-up adjustment is based on the percent change between the Consumer Price Index for all Urban Consumers (CPI-U) for the month of October in the year of the previous adjustment (or in the year of establishment, if no adjustment has been made) and the October 2015 CPI-U.
The Bureau issued an interim final rule providing for calculated catch-up adjustments on June 30, 2016 (81 FR 42478), with an effective date of August 1, 2016, and requesting comments post-promulgation. The Bureau issued a final rule affirming the catch-up adjustments set forth in the interim final rule on December 2, 2016 (81 FR 86953). The Bureau then issued a final rule making the next scheduled annual inflation adjustment for 2017 on January 23, 2017 (82 FR 7649), for 2018 on February 6, 2018 (83 FR 5192), for 2019 on April 15, 2019 (84 FR 15098), for 2020 on February 19, 2020 (85 FR 9366), for 2021 on January 28, 2021 (86 FR 7344), for 2022 on March 9, 2022 (87 FR 13153), for 2023 on March 2, 2023 (88 FR 13018), for 2024 on March 13, 2024 (89 FR 18359), and for 2025 on June 5, 2025 (90 FR 23855).
II. Calculation of 2026 Annual Adjustments
OMB recently issued guidance to assist Federal agencies in implementing the annual adjustments required by the Act.
See
April 17, 2026, Memorandum for the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies, from Russell T. Vought, Director, Office of Management and Budget, re:
Cancellation of Penalty Inflation Adjustments for 2026, Regarding the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act Improvements Act of 2015 (M-26-11).
The guidance informs agencies of the cancellation of the inflation adjustment for 2026 based on the lack of October 2025 CPI-U data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics due to the lapse in appropriations.
III. Procedural Requirements
A. Regulatory Planning and Review (E.O.s 12866 and 14192)
This rule has been determined to be not significant for purposes of E.O. 12866. This rule adjusts the level of existing civil monetary penalties and does not promulgate a new regulation defined in E.O. 14192.
B. Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. 601 et seq.)
The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) requires an agency to prepare a regulatory flexibility analysis for rules unless the agency certifies that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. The RFA applies only to rules for which an agency is required to first publish a proposed rule. See 5 U.S.C. 603(a) and 604(a). A proposed inflation adjustment rule was not published in accordance with the Act. See Section III.M, “Administrative Procedure Act,” below.
C. Congressional Review Act (CRA)
This rule is not a major rule under 5 U.S.C. 804(2). This rule:
(a) Does not have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more.
(b) Will not cause a major increase in costs or prices for consumers, individual industries, Federal, State, or local government agencies, or geographic regions.
(c) Does not have significant adverse effects on competition, employment, investment, productivity, innovation, or the ability of U.S.-based enterprises to compete with foreign-based enterprises.
D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (2 U.S.C. 1501et seq.)
This rule does not impose an unfunded mandate on State, local, or tribal governments, or the private sector of more than $100 million per year. The rule does not have a significant or unique effect on State, local, or tribal governments or the private sector. A statement containing the information required by the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (2 U.S.C. 1531et seq.) is not required.
This rule does not affect a taking of private property or otherwise have taking implications under E.O. 12630. A takings implication assessment is not requir

articles.full_text:
India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.
Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.
Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.
Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.
On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.
Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.
The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.
At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.
However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.
It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.
Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.
Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.
“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”

articles.title: The net fiscal impact of immigration should include gains from trade
articles.summary:
Immigration affects natives through both labor markets and public budgets, yet these channels are usually studied separately. We combine them in a general-equilibrium model with search-and-matching frictions, skill-specific progressive labor taxes, capital taxation and public goods, calibrated to 17 OECD countries over 2015-2019. The welfare effect on natives of a one-percentage-point increase in immigrant inflows […]
The post The net fiscal impact of immigration should include gains from ...
articles.full_text:
Immigration affects natives through both labor markets and public budgets, yet these channels are usually studied separately. We combine them in a general-equilibrium model with search-and-matching frictions, skill-specific progressive labor taxes, capital taxation and public goods, calibrated to 17 OECD countries over 2015-2019. The welfare effect on natives of a one-percentage-point increase in immigrant inflows varies in sign and size across countries, hinging on immigrants’ skill mix, immigrant-native wage gaps, resident unemployment, and tax progressivity. For inflows matching the skill composition of 2019-2024 arrivals, native welfare rises in 14 of 17 economies, and in most cases both skill groups gain, through different channels. Lower-skilled natives gain mainly from higher pre-tax earnings, driven by job creation and complementarity with skilled immigrants; higher-skilled natives gain mainly from lower labor-tax burdens. Evaluating immigration policy thus requires modeling labor-market and fiscal channels jointly: either channel alone gives an incomplete picture of who gains and why.
That is from a new NBER working paper by  Michele Battisti,   Giovanni Peri   & Eleonora Romano.  I have seen the core point here neglected so, so many times in recent discussions of the fiscal impact of immigration.  The gains from trade count too!
As a side note, I do not accept the authors’ claim that the immigrants are equally productive yet underpaid, and thus the native economy benefits from capturing that surplus.  The better mechanism is simply that immigrants boost market size, and (especially for the United States) that brings some gains from increasing returns to scale, more innovation, making the country a talent magnet, and so on.  The point holds that the gains from trade effect can be small, and it still will overwhelm what otherwise appear to be net fiscal costs.

articles.title: On Brazilian food
articles.summary:
Every now and then I will write a piece on food for Works in Progress.  Here is my piece on eating in Brazil: Brazil, like most large nations, also offers multiple cuisines. For instance you can go to Minas Gerais for pork and beans. Minas beans would be my favorite of what I have sampled, […]
The post On Brazilian food appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
Every now and then I will write a piece on food for Works in Progress.  Here is my piece on eating in Brazil:
Brazil, like most large nations, also offers multiple cuisines. For instance you can go to Minas Gerais for pork and beans. Minas beans would be my favorite of what I have sampled, surpassing Mexico. Belem serves cuisine from the Amazon region, including exotic river fish, dried shrimp, duck, and rice, with flavors from cassava, manioc, and the local fruit. You cannot get those dishes in many other places.
Feijoada is of slave origins, and is often associated with Rio de Janeiro, but it has evolved into a national dish, available almost everywhere. Think rice, black beans, collard greens, orange slices, and farofa, a kind of manioc flour, with different parts of the pig mixed in. At home I cook the vegetarian version of this dish. The coolness and sweetness of the orange go well with the sandy texture of the farofa, and the meal hardly costs anything to make.
Rio de Janeiro offers highly cosmopolitan options, and the city has a tradition of excellent French and Continental restaurants.
The best churrascarias I have had were on the outskirts of Curitiba in the south. You can get an excellent pasta meal combined with your choice of many kinds of meat, leading to an impossibly large quantity of food at your disposal. I favored these establishments more in my youth, but if you have never tried them, you are missing something.
Campo Grande, the booming agro-city in central western Brazil, has a derivative form of Okinawan soba (!) as a dining specialty. I regret that, due to a delayed flight connection, I have yet to try this apparent delicacy.
There is much more at the link, recommended.
The post On Brazilian food appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

articles.title: United Airlines CEO faces rightwing backlash after calling for US wealth tax
articles.summary: Scott Kirby says wealth inequality is a ‘danger to society’ and calls for inheritance tax in recent interviewScott Kirby, the CEO of United Airlines, is under scrutiny from conservative politicians and commentators for saying wealth inequality is a “danger to society” and calling for a national wealth and inheritance tax in a recent interview.Talking to the New York Times, Kirby was asked about the growing public distrust of CEOs and whether he felt any responsibility to quell that distrust. Con...
articles.full_text:
Scott Kirby, the CEO of United Airlines, is under scrutiny from conservative politicians and commentators for saying wealth inequality is a “danger to society” and calling for a national wealth and inheritance tax in a recent interview.
Talking to the New York Times, Kirby was asked about the growing public distrust of CEOs and whether he felt any responsibility to quell that distrust.
“We should have a national wealth tax – it won’t work by state because people will just move,” he said. “And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them.”
In response, headlines from Fox Business and the New York Post decried that Kirby made $32m in 2025. In response to Kirby’s comments, Glenn Beck, a former Fox News host, and other users on X called for a boycott of United Airlines. Jeff Landry, Louisiana’s governor, said the statement was “audacious”.
“How audacious from a guy that didn’t even build @united and makes $32 million a year,” he wrote on X, adding a link to a government website to donate money to the government. “Better yet, he should distribute his salary to the employees at the bottom of the ladder @united!”
“Let’s see you step up and place your money where your mouth is!” Landry added.
The comment comes just two weeks before voters in California will decide on a so-called “billionaire’s tax”, which would put a 5% tax on the state’s billionaires, that the wealthy have been spending millions fighting against.
Kirby was also asked about the rising cost of flying and said that high prices this year were being compared to the “artificial low” prices from the pandemic, which largely halted travel and highly disrupted the airline industry.
“We have to charge enough that it covers the cost of flying, and it’s expensive to fly airplanes,” he said.
When asked about the $70 passengers must pay to sit in an aisle or window seat if they aren’t a frequent flyer with United, Kirby responded that “the way to give everyone what they want is to charge for the services and products that those customers want,” adding: “There are customers that pay more that get more.”
Kirby also maintained that fares were still lower than in 2019 after adjusting for inflation. According to data from the labor department, the index for airline fares increased by about 20% from September 2019 to September 2026, while overall consumer prices increased by 31%.

articles.title: Saving for the machines
articles.summary:
From Jesús Fernández-Villaverde: When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, […]
The post Saving for the machines appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
From Jesús Fernández-Villaverde:
When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S. 2025 level of 23%. Therefore, slow growth might reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck. Also, the saving rate rises mainly because automation raises the capital share, not because households become thriftier. Long yields price the growth boom: the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact. In my benchmark calibration, hand-to-mouth households lose the equivalent of two-fifths to two-thirds of their consumption, while keeping them on trend temporarily costs at most a fifth of GDP.

articles.title: US judge dismisses sexual abuse lawsuit from Sam Altman’s sister
articles.summary: Ann Altman, the Open AI CEO’s sister, accused her brother of repeatedly sexually abusing her over two decades agoA judge dismissed a lawsuit filed by Sam Altman’s sister against him on Tuesday. Ann Altman accused the OpenAI CEO of repeatedly sexually abusing her more than two decades ago, which he has denied.In dismissing Ann Altman’s ⁠lawsuit, the US district judge Zachary Bluestone wrote that she had refused to appear for an independent medical examination despite warnings ⁠that failure to do ...
articles.full_text:
A judge dismissed a lawsuit filed by Sam Altman’s sister against him on Tuesday. Ann Altman accused the OpenAI CEO of repeatedly sexually abusing her more than two decades ago, which he has denied.
In dismissing Ann Altman’s lawsuit, the US district judge Zachary Bluestone wrote that she had refused to appear for an independent medical examination despite warnings that failure to do so would result in the case’s dismissal.
Laura Politi, a lawyer for Ann Altman, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Santos Perez, a lawyer who previously represented Ann Altman in the case but withdrew this month, said in a statement: “I am no longer authorized to comment on this case but I continue to believe in Annie.”
Ann Altman brought her lawsuit in St Louis, Missouri, federal court in January 2025.
Lawyers for Sam Altman did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Ann Altman accused her brother of sexually abusing and raping her between 1997 and 2006 at their family home in suburban Clayton, Missouri, starting when she was three and he was 12. She said the last acts of sexual abuse and rape occurred when Sam Altman was an adult. He is now 41.
The Altman family has said Ann Altman has mental health challenges and received financial support. Sam Altman has said she began accusing him on social media of sexual abuse after the family rejected her demands for more funds.
